#614. A surprising vitamin A discovery is changing what scientists know about vision

Scientists at Johns Hopkins University have uncovered a surprising role for a vitamin A derivative in the development of human vision. Their research reveals how this molecule works alongside thyroid hormones to help form the part of the eye responsible for our sharpest sight, challenging a scientific explanation that has stood for roughly 30 years.

The discovery centers on an unexpected transformation that occurs in the developing retina before birth. Certain cells that initially detect blue light appear to change into cells sensitive to red and green light, helping create the specialized arrangement needed for clear central vision.

Published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the findings could reshape scientists' understanding of how human eyes develop. They may also help advance research into future treatments for macular degeneration, glaucoma, and other conditions that cause vision loss.

"This is a key step toward understanding the inner workings of the center of the retina, a critical part of the eye and the first to fail in people with macular degeneration," said Robert J. Johnston Jr., an associate professor of biology at Johns Hopkins University who led the study. "By better understanding this region and developing organoids that mimic its function, we hope to one day grow and transplant these tissues to restore vision."

How Scientists Recreated the Developing Human Retina

To investigate how human vision forms, Johnston and his colleagues turned to an innovative laboratory technique they have helped develop over the past several years. Instead of relying entirely on animal experiments, they grew miniature versions of human retinal tissue called organoids.

These small clusters of cells, grown from fetal cells, reproduce important features of developing human tissue. By observing the retinal organoids over several months, the scientists could follow changes that would otherwise be extremely difficult to study during pregnancy.

Their attention focused on the foveola, a tiny region at the very center of the retina. The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye that converts incoming light into signals the brain can interpret. Within it, the foveola plays an especially important role in detailed central vision, which allows people to read, recognize faces, and distinguish fine details.

Although the foveola occupies only a small fraction of the retina, it is involved in approximately 50% of human visual perception, according to the researchers.

The Surprising Secret Behind Sharp Human Vision

One of the keys to understanding the foveola is a group of specialized light-detecting cells called cones. Unlike rod cells, which are particularly important for seeing in dim light, cones support daytime vision and allow us to perceive color.

Humans have three types of cone cells, each most sensitive to different wavelengths of light. These are commonly described as blue, green, and red cones. By comparing signals from these different cells, the brain can distinguish a remarkably broad range of colors.

However, the cones are not distributed evenly throughout the retina. The foveola contains red and green cones but lacks blue cones, which are found in other retinal regions. This precise arrangement is essential for the exceptionally sharp vision produced by the center of the eye.

For decades, researchers have struggled to explain how this pattern develops. One major obstacle is that commonly studied animals, including mice and fish, do not share the same retinal organization found in humans. That makes it difficult to use traditional animal models to investigate how these specialized cells develop.

The laboratory-grown human retinas offered a new opportunity to solve this longstanding mystery.

Vitamin A and Thyroid Hormones Trigger a Remarkable Change

The researchers discovered evidence that the arrangement of cones in the foveola develops through two coordinated processes. Together, they determine which types of cells form in the central retina and how some of those cells change as development continues.

During weeks 10 through 12 of fetal development, a small number of blue cones are initially present in the foveola. By week 14, however, these cells appear to have transformed into red and green cones.

The team identified two important chemical influences behind this process.

The first involves retinoic acid, a molecule produced from vitamin A. Retinoic acid helps regulate how cells develop and specialize throughout the body. In the developing retina, the breakdown of this molecule limits the formation of blue cones in the central region.

The second influence comes from thyroid hormones, which are best known for regulating metabolism but also have crucial roles in growth and development. In this case, the hormones appear to encourage the remaining blue cones to change into red and green cones.

"First, retinoic acid helps set the pattern. Then, thyroid hormone plays a role in converting the leftover cells," Johnston said. "That's very important because if you have those blue cones in there, you don't see as well."

Importantly, the discovery concerns how vitamin A signaling helps guide eye development before birth. It does not establish that taking vitamin A supplements can improve sharp vision in adults.

A Discovery That Challenges a 30-Year-Old Theory

The results offer a striking alternative to an explanation that has influenced vision research for decades.

Under the longstanding model, blue cones that initially appear in the foveola were thought to move away as the retina developed. Scientists generally assumed that once these cells became a particular type of cone, their identities remained fixed.

The new findings suggest something different. Rather than simply relocating, at least some blue cones may undergo a change in identity, becoming red or green cones as the eye develops.

"The main model in the field from about 30 years ago was that somehow the few blue cones you get in that region just move out of the way, that these cells decide what they're going to be, and they remain this type of cell forever," Johnston said. "We can't really rule that out yet, but our data supports a different model. These cells actually convert over time, which is really surprising."

The researchers have not completely ruled out the possibility that some cells migrate. Nevertheless, their observations support the idea that developing cone cells have more flexibility than previously recognized.

That possibility could fundamentally change how scientists study the formation of human color vision and the development of the retina's most specialized regions.

Could the Discovery Help Scientists Restore Lost Vision?

Beyond explaining how healthy eyes develop, the findings could have important implications for treating diseases that damage the retina.

One particularly promising application involves macular degeneration, a major cause of central vision loss, especially among older adults. The disease damages the macula, the retinal region responsible for detailed central vision, and can severely interfere with reading, driving, and recognizing faces. Although treatments can slow or manage certain forms of the disease, there is currently no cure.

Understanding how the retina creates its specialized light-sensitive cells could eventually help scientists produce healthy replacements in the laboratory.

Johnston's team is now working to improve its retinal organoids so they more closely reproduce the structure and function of the human eye. The long-term goal is to develop precisely controlled populations of photoreceptors, the cells that detect light, for potential transplantation into damaged retinas.

Katarzyna Hussey, a study author and former doctoral student in Johnston's laboratory, believes this approach could open an important new direction for vision restoration. Hussey is now a molecular and cell biologist at CiRC Biosciences, a cell therapy company in Chicago.

"The goal with using this organoid tech is to eventually make an almost made-to-order population of photoreceptors. A big avenue of potential is cell replacement therapy to introduce healthy cells that can reintegrate into the eye and potentially restore that lost vision," said Hussey.

The idea is to introduce healthy cells that could integrate with existing retinal tissue and potentially replace functions lost to disease. Achieving that goal would require researchers to demonstrate that transplanted cells can survive, connect properly with the eye's existing circuitry, and function safely.

Hussey emphasized that the technology remains far from routine clinical use, with extensive development and testing still necessary.

"These are very long-term experiments, and of course we'd need to do optimizations for safety and efficacy studies prior to moving into the clinic. But it's a viable journey."

For now, the discovery provides something fundamental: a clearer explanation of how the human eye develops its remarkable ability to see fine details. By revealing how vitamin A signaling and thyroid hormones help shape the retina, scientists have taken another step toward understanding vision at its earliest stages and potentially finding ways to restore it when disease strikes.

#611. Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness

A surprising discovery made with NASA's Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from darkness. The findings suggest that powerful explosions from dying stars may have actually interfered with a process scientists once believed they helped drive.

An international research team, including astronomers from the University of Michigan, found that powerful winds produced by exploding stars can prevent ultraviolet radiation from escaping galaxies. This is the opposite of what a widely accepted theory had predicted, and it could change how scientists understand one of the most important transformations in cosmic history.

The discovery, published in Nature Astronomy, offers new clues about how the universe became transparent to ultraviolet light roughly 13 billion years ago.

How the Early Universe Emerged From Its Cosmic Fog

During the first billion years after the Big Bang, vast amounts of neutral hydrogen filled the space between galaxies. This hydrogen formed a kind of cosmic fog that absorbed ultraviolet radiation, preventing that light from traveling freely across the universe.

That changed during a period known as reionization, which began approximately 13 billion years ago. Intense radiation from early galaxies gradually transformed the hydrogen by stripping electrons from its atoms, leaving behind positively charged protons and free electrons.

As more hydrogen became ionized, ultraviolet light could travel much farther through intergalactic space. This transformation helped establish the relatively transparent universe that astronomers observe today.

"Eventually, when it ionized the majority of hydrogen filling intergalactic space, that was the end of reionization and we see the universe today," said Cody Carr, a postdoctoral researcher in the University of Michigan's Department of Astronomy. "We call reionization the last major phase transition of the universe."

Despite its enormous importance, astronomers still do not fully understand which objects supplied the radiation responsible for reionization or how enough of that radiation managed to escape from early galaxies.

"We don't know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved," said Carr, who conducted and led the research while working as a postdoctoral scholar at Zhejiang University in China, before joining the University of Michigan. "We know that it took place, but we don't have complete answers to those questions."

Hubble Challenges a Leading Theory About Exploding Stars

For years, one prominent explanation centered on supernovae, the powerful explosions that occur when certain stars reach the ends of their lives. These explosions can generate enormous winds that sweep through galaxies, pushing gas and other material outward.

Scientists proposed that these winds cleared pathways through the gas surrounding young stars, allowing ultraviolet radiation to escape into the space between galaxies. Once outside, that radiation could help break apart the neutral hydrogen responsible for the universe's ancient fog.

However, new observations from Hubble suggest that this explanation may have the process backward.

Rather than opening routes for radiation to escape, the researchers found that stronger galactic winds were associated with less escaping ionizing radiation. The observations indicate that the winds generated by supernovae can actually make it harder for the radiation to leave a galaxy.

"Basically, how these galaxies were leaking ionizing radiation isn't what we thought," Carr said.

The results lend support to a different possibility. Radiation from young, massive stars may escape their galaxies before those stars explode as supernovae and generate large winds that reshape the surrounding environment.

"Our observations show that these photons are escaping before galactic winds form," Carr said.

Photons are individual packets of light energy. In this case, the researchers are interested in ultraviolet photons energetic enough to ionize hydrogen, making them essential to understanding how the early universe became transparent.

What Hubble Discovered in Nearby Starburst Galaxies

To investigate how radiation escapes, the international team used the Hubble Space Telescope to examine nearby starburst galaxies. These are galaxies experiencing exceptionally intense periods of star formation, making them useful modern examples of the kinds of galaxies believed to have contributed to reionization.

Hubble, a NASA mission launched with contributions from the European Space Agency, allowed researchers to study the light coming from these galaxies in detail.

The team examined their spectra, which reveal how much light is present at different wavelengths. By studying the patterns in those spectra, astronomers can learn about the gas surrounding stars and determine how quickly it is moving.

Gas absorbs particular wavelengths of light, creating recognizable dips in a galaxy's spectrum. The locations and shapes of these dips provide clues about the speed and movement of galactic winds.

When the researchers compared wind speeds with the amount of ionizing radiation escaping from each galaxy, they uncovered a surprising relationship. Galaxies with the fastest winds allowed the smallest fraction of ionizing radiation to escape.

That result directly challenges the expectation that stronger winds should clear away more gas and make it easier for radiation to reach intergalactic space.

"It appears that energy input from supernovae has stirred up the surroundings and increased, rather than decreased, the coverage of neutral gas and dust that suppresses ionizing radiation escape," said Stephan McCandliss, a senior author of the study and director of the Center for Astrophysical Sciences at Johns Hopkins University.

In other words, instead of clearing a path for ultraviolet light, energy from exploding stars appears to redistribute gas and dust in ways that can block more of it.

Young Stars May Hold the Key to Cosmic Reionization

Although large galactic winds appear to suppress escaping radiation, smaller winds and other activity around young stars could still help create openings in the surrounding gas.

These processes may occur before the first supernova explosions, giving radiation a chance to escape while conditions are more favorable.

The findings suggest that astronomers may need to pay greater attention to what happens during the earliest stages of star formation, rather than focusing primarily on the effects of exploding stars.

Carr and his colleagues are seeking additional observing time with Hubble to examine more galaxies and investigate whether the same patterns appear elsewhere. More observations could help establish how important the activity of young stars is in allowing ionizing radiation to escape.

The results also have implications for computer simulations of the early universe. These simulations attempt to recreate how galaxies formed, how gas moved through them, and how radiation eventually transformed the hydrogen filling intergalactic space.

"Supernovae play a central role in cosmological hydrodynamic simulations that explain how ionizing radiation escapes from galaxies," said Renyue Cen, a senior author of the study and professor and director of the Center for Cosmology and Computational Astrophysics at Zhejiang University. "Our findings highlight the need to examine how radiation and winds from young stars shape the surrounding gas before the first supernovae explode."

By accounting more accurately for these early interactions between stars, radiation, and gas, researchers may be able to build better models of how reionization unfolded.

The discovery does not yet settle the question of what caused the universe's last major phase transition. However, it provides an important new clue, suggesting that the radiation that helped lift the universe's ancient fog may have escaped galaxies before powerful stellar explosions began to alter their surroundings.

International Research Collaboration and Funding

The research brought together nearly 30 scientists from more than a dozen institutions around the world. Sally Oey, a professor of astronomy at the University of Michigan, also contributed to the study.

The project received additional financial support from Zhejiang University, the Zhejiang Provincial Top-Level Research Support Program, the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities in Spain, the European Regional Development Fund, and the European Union's Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Program.

The research was also supported in part by federal funding from NASA and the U.S. National Science Foundation. Additional support for the Hubble Space Telescope observations came through a grant administered by the Space Telescope Science Institute.

#608. Marc Lore’s Wonder bets on Texas, automation and user-built restaurants as it mulls IPO

Less than a decade after its founding, food startup Wonder has seen its footprint and valuation soar.

Still, the company has even more ambitious plans ahead, like a subscription program to let diners run their own "restaurants," an aggressive expansion in Texas and a potential initial public offering.

Created by serial entrepreneur Marc Lore in 2018, Wonder advertises itself as "the best restaurants from across the country, all in one place." Diners can place takeout or delivery orders from its food hall-style locations on the Wonder-branded app or third-party platforms, including Grubhub, which Wonder now owns.

As Lore described it to CNBC, "Wonder is a vertically integrated food technology platform to make great food more accessible."

To achieve its goal, Wonder plans to open locations in urban, suburban and rural areas nationwide and aims to keep prices lower than the cost of delivered groceries. Thanks to its ownership of Grubhub, Wonder customers who order through the startup's app don't have to pay delivery fees, and its menu prices aren't inflated to cover the cost of commission fees to the delivery platform. Plus, Wonder is automating some of its kitchen functions, like assembling salads and bowls and soon sauces and beverages.

The company aims for food preparation and delivery to be fully autonomous by 2040, Lore said.

Now, Wonder has to convince diners its platform built on cost savings and choice makes it worth their while in a competitive industry.

Lore's lofty vision for Wonder has helped the company raise $3.3 billion to date, from investors like DoorDash, Alphabet's venture arm and Gwyneth Paltrow. Its Series D fundraising round earlier this year raised its pre-money valuation to $9 billion — just under sandwich chain Subway's sale price two years ago.

Wonder's next pitch to investors could be on an IPO road show, assuming that the window for companies across industries to go public reopens in the coming months.

"[The mission] is really why I want to go public and raise the capital that it'll take to build that kind of generational business, also to have a public currency to be able to do more M&A," Lore said. "But I can't talk about timing."

Lore's expertise lies in e-commerce, not restaurants.

He helped found the parent company of Diapers.com and sold it in 2010 to Amazon for $545 million. Just six years later, Walmart paid about $3 billion for his follow-up venture, Jet.com. Lore stayed at the retailer until 2021 to accelerate Walmart's e-commerce growth.

Basketball fans might also recognize Lore as an owner of the Minnesota Timberwolves. In 2021, he and baseball legend Alex Rodriguez agreed to buy the team for $1.5 billion, although the deal was not finalized until 2025. Lore recently struck a deal to shrink his investment to a minority stake "to focus on his business," Rodriguez said in a statement in August, referring to Wonder.

Lore's latest startup began with the idea of bringing food delivery to consumers' homes through sprinter vans outfitted with mobile kitchens. The trucks lasted roughly two years before Wonder phased them out in favor of brick-and-mortar locations, which could serve more food options and lower costs.

Lore's successful track record has helped him win over investors for Wonder.

"I joke around at GV that I do enterprise software investing, AI investing and anything that Marc Lore is running as an active CEO," said Dave Munichiello, managing partner of Alphabet's venture capital arm GV, who has known Lore since his Diapers.com days and invested in Jet.com through GV.

Lore himself thinks that his vision is the reason for Wonder's billions of dollars of funding.

"Everybody eats," he said. "It's defensible from AI."

Wonder has spent more than $1 billion on acquisitions, not including the deals where financial details were not disclosed. Its purchases of Grubhub, delivery and logistics provider Relay, meal-kit provider Blue Apron and buzzy New York restaurant concepts have been expensive.

But Lore said he sees a "tremendous total addressable market" for Wonder if it's able to sell high-quality food at accessible prices, particularly in exurban and rural areas with few dining options beyond fast food and gas stations.

From Virginia to Massachusetts, 170 Wonder storefronts have appeared over the last three years. Next year, the company plans to enter Texas for the first time — with a goal of at least 100 locations in the state by the end of 2027.

Wonder prepares its food at commissary kitchens, then transports it to each individual location, where employees unseal, cook and finish the menu items. Its storefronts are all electric, without gas or venting, so Wonder can quickly move into a new space and cut down on renovations and red tape.

Its locations serve menu items from more than two dozen "restaurants," including Dabba Indian Kitchen, Tejas Barbecue and Pop Salad. Celebrity chefs including Bobby Flay, Michael Symon and Marcus Samuelsson receive up-front payments and equity in Wonder to let the company use their names for some of those concepts. More recent additions include acquisitions such as Blue Ribbon Fried Chicken and Salt Hank's, brands with established followings.

With its wide variety of options housed under one roof, Wonder has drawn comparisons to ghost kitchens, the once-buzzy startups without dine-in seating that flamed out as food delivery orders fell after the Covid pandemic. Once considered a potential disruptor to the restaurant industry, ghost kitchen companies such as Kitchen United have sought bankruptcy protection and wound down their operations.

"You can see there's a front of house [in the] brick and mortar," he said. "You'll see people at lunchtime, sitting there enjoying lunch, so it's not ghost-y in that way. But I think it's also just in the fact that we're vertically integrated."

Wonder has never marketed itself as a ghost kitchen, instead calling itself "a new kind of food hall" or a "modern food court" before landing on a "vertically integrated food technology platform."

Starting Nov. 17, the company plans to take the next step with Wonder Create. Influencers, entrepreneurs and brands can pay $10 a month to start their own "restaurant" based out of a Wonder location and earn a portion of the revenue from orders. Artificial intelligence will help them make their brand, including name, logo, pricing and recipes.

"It could be a restaurant for you and your friends, or you could be an influencer that has a following," Lore said.

He wants Wonder Create to democratize restaurant ownership — minus the capital, overhead costs or oversight of kitchen operations. The platform will eventually be available to the public, with users deciding menu items based on Wonder's pantry.

Besides Wonder Create, the company is also using AI for another initiative. MEL, a proprietary AI platform, can use a customer's health information, like data from an Oura ring or Whoop tracker or even blood biomarkers, to prepare breakfast, lunch and dinner for its user.

MEL is not currently available to Wonder customers, although Lore uses AI to advise his own meals, like the chicken muffin he ate for breakfast on a Tuesday in October.

While Wonder has won over venture capitalists, the battle for diners' stomachs and wallets is tougher.

Budget-conscious consumers have been dining out less often and becoming pickier when they do so. And while food delivery is still more popular than it was before the pandemic, consumers have pulled back on delivery orders compared with their Covid-era peak. Fees and high menu prices, which offset eateries' commission fees with apps, make delivery even more expensive than dining at a restaurant.

Plus, some consumers are skeptical about Wonder more specifically. Posts on social media decry the company's food quality and its funding from venture capital.

"It's OK, but it's just average," Amir Ings, a 27-year-old living in Philadelphia, said in a TikTok reviewing an order of three tacos from Wonder in late 2025. "My expectations were already in the gutter — it's not as bad as I thought it was going to be, but it's still not great. And I paid like $16 for this, but it should have been no more than $8."

Lore told CNBC that Wonder receives thousands of reviews every day from customers, rating the taste, temperature and portion size of their orders on a scale from 1 to 10. Wonder starts its board meetings by talking about taste scores, Munichiello said.

"We're maniacally focused on food quality .... We're constantly iterating on the meals that score lower, and see over time, the last 12 months, our taste scores have improved, our Google reviews have improved," Lore said. "I do expect food quality to improve as we scale, which is not always the case."

Despite lackluster reviews on social media, Wonder has fans. Based on transaction data from Indagari, Wonder had a higher weighted average retention rate — how likely a diner is to return — and higher lifetime value — how much a customer has spent over time — than Cava and Sweetgreen.

Plus, Wonder has succeeded with locations in the most competitive markets for restaurants in the country.

"They made this company work well in the hardest place in the country to stand up this model: New York," Munichiello said. "You have so much choice in New York."

Ultimately, Wonder wants to win over the rest of the U.S. — and public market investors.

In March, the company hired Gabrielle Scheibe Rabinovitch, previously at payment processor Worldpay, as its chief financial officer as it prepares to go public.

Lore declined to comment on the timing of a potential IPO to CNBC, although he has previously told Fortune that the company will be "ready and prepared to go public early next year."

Since buying Blue Apron and Grubhub, Wonder has been operating at a financial loss, The Information previously reported. It plans to bring down the price of its meals by leaning into automation and drone delivery. In the long term, that plan could cut costs, although laying the groundwork won't be cheap.

In recent years, investors have grown less tolerant of startups pursuing growth at all costs, according to Avery Marquez, director of investment strategies at Renaissance Capital. To sway investors, unprofitable companies have to show they are taking steps toward profitability — or that the growth will continue long after the IPO.

#607. Scientists reveal a hidden snakebite crisis killing up to 513,000 people a year

Not every snakebite injects venom. When venom enters the body, however, it can cause snake envenoming. This is a potentially fatal condition and it mostly affects poor rural communities across tropical and subtropical regions who don’t have easy access to medical care.

As researchers with decades of combined experience in snakebite and tropical disease epidemiology, we came to realise that snake envenoming faces a data crisis. Over half of the countries where venomous snakes pose a threat don’t keep count of how many people are bitten or envenomed.

In rural sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia, many victims live hours away from the nearest clinic, lack transport, or seek care from traditional healers. As a result, their cases are never captured in national health statistics.

To bridge this massive gap, we conducted a study to map the global burden of snake envenoming and related deaths.

We looked at data from 79 countries by reviewing studies published up to March 31, 2025. This allowed us to update the findings from our milestone 2008 global burden study. To fill the remaining data gaps, we built a geostatistical model that combines real-world data with local environmental and socioeconomic factors. This allowed us to estimate envenoming and fatality rates.

We conclude from our findings that snake envenoming is a public health crisis on a far greater scale than official statistics have shown. Our results show that sub-Saharan Africa bears the heaviest toll.

The World Health Organization has set an ambitious target to halve snakebite mortality and disability by 2030. Mapping the problem at the country level is the first crucial step.

To overcome the lack of reliable data, we turned to a model-based geostatistics framework.

To understand how this modelling works, think of it as predicting invisible patterns by combining known data points with environmental signals. Instead of assuming data for every region, this modelling uses statistical probability to calculate a range of likely outcomes based on environmental signals.

We fed our model with data including climate, snake species richness and socioeconomic indicators. The model then calculated the probability of snakebites occurring in specific locations, even where official health records were completely blank.

By comparing different data sources (including hospital-reported data and regional statistics) against ground level community-survey data, our framework allowed us to account for unreported snake envenomings. It produced both a baseline floor and a potential upper ceiling for snake envenomings and fatalities.

Based on this, we estimate that at least 2.1 million people experience snake envenoming each year globally. The true number could be high as 7 million. Using our model, which adjusts for substantial under-reporting, annual deaths may range from 274,000 to 513,000.

The geographic distribution of this burden is uneven. Our research shows that sub-Saharan Africa alone accounts for 45% of all global envenomings and fatalities. That burden has likely been underestimated for decades. People in sub-Saharan Africa experience snake envenoming and death at nearly three times the rate seen in south Asia.

Countries like Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Ethiopia face a high burden, driven by dense rural populations and high exposure in agricultural fields.

The reasons sub-Saharan Africa suffers such disproportionate harm are structural rather than accidental.

Firstly, the continent hosts a rich diversity of medically important venomous species. These include saw-scaled vipers (Echis spp.), puff adders (Bitis arietans), African cobras (Naja spp.) and mambas (Dendroaspis spp.). They are responsible for substantial morbidity and mortality across the continent.

Secondly, millions of rural agricultural workers labor in open fields without protective boots and walk on unlit footpaths at night. When a bite occurs, fragile health systems, long travel distances to regional facilities and the high cost or total absence of effective antivenom mean a treatable medical emergency can quickly become fatal. Similar conditions exist in parts of Asia.

We estimate that over 800,000 survivors are left with long-term physical disabilities each year, including amputations and other permanent impairments. These disabilities can reduce household income, increase healthcare costs and push already vulnerable farming families deeper into poverty.

Meeting the World Health Organization’s goal requires moving away from guesswork and using spatial risk data to guide real-world policy.

By identifying high-risk hotspots, governments and global health partners can strategically stockpile antivenom where it is needed most, train primary healthcare workers in high-burden rural zones and improve rapid transport infrastructure.

Snake envenoming has remained hidden for too long. Better data cannot solve the problem, but can help ensure that antivenom, healthcare services and prevention efforts reach the communities that need them most.

Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Dileepa Ediriweera, Health Data Scientist, Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

On the first day of his farewell tour in China, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier urged the German business community to act with confidence in the Chinese market.

"When you travel in China, you're amazed at how highly Germany and German technology are still valued here," he said in Hefei. "That's why we can act with confidence in these markets."

Steinmeier did not bring any companies with him to China as part of his delegation, as his final trip was intended to focus on culture and science.

Nevertheless, the first day of the trip in Hefei, the capital of Anhui Province, revolved primarily around the economy. Steinmeier visited the Volkswagen China Technology Company (VCTC). About three years ago, Europe's largest automaker opened a research center for electric mobility there, which today employs 3,000 people.

Johannes Volkmann, a lawmaker accompanying Steinmeier in China, warned that the German economy must not "lose its leadership in innovation."

"I'm taking this call to action with me from here to do more to improve competitive conditions at home," he said, adding that Germany must avoid creating new dependencies "by allowing innovation and value creation to take place only outside Europe."

Steinmeier called for Europe to reposition itself and reorganize its economic instruments with its growing trade deficit with China in mind.

"The trade surplus that China is accumulating naturally causes us concern because the successful model of economic cooperation is becoming unbalanced," he said. "We must strive to ensure that economic cooperation does not come to an end, but that it continues — to the mutual benefit of both sides."

Germany's trade deficit with China amounted to just under €90 billion ($100 billion) in 2025. According to the Federal Statistical Office, China exported goods worth €170.6 billion to Germany, and German exports to China amounted to €81.3 billion.

Across the 27-member EU, the deficit amounted to almost €197 billion in the first half of 2026, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic.

Additional reporting by Rosalia Romaniec in Hefei.

A German court denied a defense request to end the trial of a former Ukrainian army officer who stands accused of sabotaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines.

Serhii Kuznietsov, 50, went on trial this month at the Hamburg state court, charged with causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public services and being an "accomplice to war crimes" by attacking civilian infrastructure.

Prosecutors accuse him of being the ringleader of the destruction, considered one of Europe's biggest acts of post-World War II sabotage. He is alleged to have carried out the explosions together with six others.

His lawyers said the charges should be dismissed, arguing that, as a former soldier, Kuznietsov was obligated by Ukrainian law not to speak for national security reasons and could face severe penalties in Ukraine if he did. They argued that, under German law, anyone who cannot speak on his or her own behalf cannot be convicted.

The Hamburg court ruled Kuznietsov's defense was not limited under German law and that freedom to testify is not limited by a foreign country's conditions of service.

The undersea explosions on September 26, 2022, damaged the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, which brought Russian natural gas to Germany until Moscow cut off supplies in August 2022.

The blasts also damaged the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never went into service. Germany suspended the pipeline's certification process shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Italian authorities detained Kuznietsov last year. He was publicly named in extradition proceedings that led to his transfer to Germany in November.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has denied allegations that his country was involved in the pipeline blasts.

German carmaker Mercedes-Benz has cut its forecast for 2026, with difficult market conditions in China and higher fourth-quarter cost expectations set to negatively impact profits, the company said on Tuesday.

Markets were quick to take note of the announcement, and Mercedes shares dropped 3.4% in trading on Tuesday morning.

The move makes Mercedes the third big German carmaker to lower its outlook for 2026 after BMW and VW took similar steps.

Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Kaellenius has called on German employees to work more without pay while also expanding manufacturing operations in Hungary, where he said costs are about 70% lower than in Germany.

Mercedes currently expects an adjusted car profit margin of 2% to 3% in 2026, compared to the 3% to 5% in the previous guidance.

Mercedes vehicle deliveries in China — last year already at their lowest level since 2016 — fell a further 29% in the nine months to the end of September.

Mercedes also released third-quarter figures earlier than planned, which showed that the company generated just €172 million ($191 million) in free cash flow from its vehicle business, down on the €422 million forecast by financial market experts.

Before interest and tax, Mercedes posted an operating profit of €1.77 billion — more than double the €750 million recorded a year earlier, according to the preliminary figures. But last year's stats were significantly impacted by one-time expenses, especially related to job cuts and legal disputes.

The German agency responsible for finding a final repository for nuclear waste (BGE) has eliminated five states from its search.

Berlin, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony and Saarland were deemed unsuitable for long-term radioactive waste storage.

In a report issued Tuesday, the BGE said it had limited its search to 5% of Germany, down from 25% in 2025. The federal agency aims to suggest suitable locations for final evaluation by the end of 2027.

Regions in northern, northwestern, southern and eastern Germany remain under consideration as locations for final storage facilities.

Germany's nuclear waste is currently stored in 16 above-ground interim storage facilities.

The BGE assessments evaluate regions' geological conditions and their ability to safely contain highly radioactive material. Granite, salt, and clay are generally considered potentially suitable types of rock and areas with damaged or compromised subsurface conditions, places with mines or volcanos have been active, are not eligible as final disposal sites.

Germany needs to find a repository for approximately 27,000 cubic meters of highly radioactive nuclear waste generated over more than 60 years of nuclear power generation. The site is expected to ensure safety for 1 million years. The last German nuclear power plants were decommissioned in April 2023.

BGE said its goal remains finding the site that offers the highest level of safety for highly radioactive waste.

The agency's recommendations, however, are not legally binding and it will be up to German lawmakers to determine the final disposal site.

Convicted right-wing terrorist Beate Zschäpe's request for early release from prison was denied with a court ruling that she would remain behind bars for at least nine more years.

Munich's Higher Regional Court on Tuesday set her minimum term at at least 24 years and refused to suspend the sentence to probation. By determining her guilt to be particularly severe, the court effectively ruled out her release after 15 years, which, including her time in pretrial detention, would have expired this year.

The Munich court said Zschäpe, currently 51, still had a good chance of leaving prison alive.

The decision is not yet legally binding, and the defense and the Federal Prosecutor's Office can appeal.

Zschäpe had been sentenced to life in prison in 2018 as an accomplice in the National Socialist Underground (NSU) murders that killed 10 people, mainly individuals with an immigrant background as well as a police officer.

The terror group went undetected for a decade. Zschäpe's fellow NSU members, Uwe Mundlos and Uwe Böhnhardt, injured several people with bomb attacks in Cologne and killed themselves to avoid arrest in 2011.

Under normal conditions, a convict who receives a life sentence in Germany can apply for parole after 15 years.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, along with his counterparts from France, Italy, Poland and the UK, authored an op-ed calling Russia "the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability."

In the article, published online and in Tuesday's Tagesspiegel newspaper, the defense ministers wrote they "share a deep conviction" that European countries need to do more to ensure their own security and aim to build "a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO."

The ministers, however, added that the United States would remain an "indispensable ally."

The pronouncement comes as many in Europe are wary of US President Donald Trump's commitment to the NATO military alliance.

The US leader has threatened to leave the group and to seize control of Greenland, a territory of fellow NATO member Denmark. US presidents have repeatedly called for European NATO members to contribute more to the alliance's military capabilities.

As US support for Ukraine also appears to waver, the five defense ministers reiterated their political, military and financial support for Kyiv as it fights of Russia's full-scale invasion.

"We must assert our interests in an international environment shaped by renewed great-power rivalry," Merz said.

With a view to unpredictable tariffs imposed by the United States under President Donald Trump and trade restrictions from China, Merz emphasized the stability offered by Germany and the rest of Europe.

"This is a deliberate counterpoint to what we are currently seeing. We want to do things differently, and we want to show that there is a better way," Merz said, adding that Europe sought to expand partnerships to increase free trade with open competition, reliability and a rules-based order.

He also called for increased international investment and cooperation.

"Under the federal government I lead, investment opportunities will be continuously improved," Merz said following a meeting with Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong. "I encounter a great deal of confidence here in Germany and in Europe as locations for investment."

The German leader called for a new free-trade agreement between the 27-member European Union and the Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), comprising 12 countries across five continents, including Australia, Canada, Japan, Mexico and the United Kingdom. Neither the United States nor China is part of the CPTPP.

For his part, Wong said investment in Germany and Europe would continue.

"Many of our investors, including our sovereign wealth funds, have been investing in Germany for a long time," Wong said. "They will continue to invest because they are confident that, in the long term, Germany and Europe have potential."

#605. White Dwarfs Aren’t Just White. Scientists Discover Dying Stars Turning Pink and Green

The realm of stars resembles a fairy tale. In it, we find giants, supergiants, and also many dwarfs. Rather like the flames of a fire, most stars’ colors are based on temperature. Cooler stars look orange, sun-like stars appear white, and the hottest ones shine light blue. However, there are exceptions, and astronomers have recently discovered some among the class of stars known as white dwarfs.

At the end of their lives, stars with a mass similar to the sun expand and turn into red giants. Subsequently, they shed their gaseous envelope, creating a planetary nebula that we can admire through telescopes. In place of the star, a white dwarf remains—a highly condensed object the approximate volume of the Earth but the mass of the sun.

Initially, white dwarfs have extremely high temperatures, and so the first ones discovered shone from white to light blue. That’s how they got their name. But according to a new study published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments, the world of white dwarfs is actually far more colorful—with some stars turning pink, green, and even purple.

The researchers posit that density is the deciding factor. The atmospheres of the coolest white dwarfs can reach a density of approximately 1 gram per cubic centimeter. That’s roughly the same density as water, which may not sound like much, but it’s packed for a star, this being about a million times denser than the sun’s atmosphere. Under these conditions, any trace elements like carbon, calcium, and sodium interact with the surrounding dense helium plasma and absorb light across a wider range of colors.

Material from ancient planetary systems also plays a role. The closest planets can perish in the fiery embrace of the red giant phase. Other planets, and especially asteroids, begin to collide and migrate toward the dead star. Fragments of these bodies then integrate into the white dwarf's atmosphere.

Through a hobbyist’s telescope, a white dwarf looks just like any other faint star. However, if observed up close, their colors would be much more varied. Carbon-rich white dwarfs tend to be pink or purple. According to calculations, white dwarfs whose atmospheres have been enriched with material from shattered asteroids or other bodies will exhibit yellow and, in some cases, green shades. The coolest white dwarfs are often a baby blue, which is caused by hydrogen and helium atoms colliding in their extremely dense atmospheres.

One example is the star WD J1330+6435. With a temperature of around 4,000 degrees Celsius, it has accumulated rocky material from its planetary system, enriching its atmosphere with calcium, lithium, and sodium. These elements give it a light chartreuse color, making it the first known green star in our galaxy.

Another white dwarf, WD J1011+2845, has a massive amount of carbon in its atmosphere. Almost all of its radiation is concentrated at wavelengths exceeding 600 nanometers, giving it a salmon-pink color. Meanwhile, the white dwarf WD J902-2010 leans toward the more bubblegum end of the spectrum.

However, there’s no reason to expect white dwarfs to start getting renamed, because most of these stars are, in fact, white. For this study, the authors examined 152 white dwarfs located within 65 light-years of Earth. Only five of them showed unusual coloration, suggesting that approximately one in thirty white dwarfs in the universe shines with unusually colored light.

This might seem like an expected result, but scientists previously assumed that white dwarfs were predominantly blue. That assumption may reflect bias in sampling the night sky. The hottest white dwarfs are also typically the brightest and can, therefore, be seen from greater distances. Because they’re easier to observe, many studies end up over-representing blue stars.

While you won’t be able to see the nearest white dwarf with the naked eye either, you can at least look in its direction. Sirius B is the companion to the brightest star in Earth’s night sky. During winter, Sirius is easy to spot shining brightly above the eastern horizon. Sirius B belongs to the group of “more boring” white dwarfs—its temperature hovers around 25,000 Kelvin, giving it a light blue color.

#603. Scientists discover mysterious seahorse lookalikes that no one has ever seen alive

At first glance it looks exactly like a seahorse. It has the same horse-shaped head tilted down from the body, the same curled and grasping tail, and in the males a fully enclosed pouch for brooding the young.

But this little fish, no longer than your thumb, is not a seahorse, as we report in our new study published in the Journal of Lost Species. This is Australyichthys aegis, a newly described fish from the deep reefs off southern Australia. We have given it the common name helmethead sea muppet, after the domed, helmet-like crest on its head.

Its scientific name follows the same idea: in Greek mythology the aegis was a protective shield. Together with its two relatives, the bullneck sea muppet (A. minotaur) and the paradoxical sea muppet (A. paradoxus), it makes up a small group we nickname the sea muppets.

All three, we have now shown, belong on their own branch of the family tree. The seahorse look has arisen more than once, and these fish are a case of it evolving well away from the true seahorses. That evidence had been sitting in museum drawers, misfiled, for decades.

You will not find these fish while scuba diving.

Every known specimen was brought up by accident, caught in trawl nets or dredges working the seafloor between about 50 and 125 meters down. The single specimen of A. aegis came up in 2006 near the Gambier Islands, at the mouth of South Australia’s Spencer Gulf.

The dredge that caught it was sampling for small shelled animals known as brachiopods during a natural history expedition. Because that expedition was after invertebrates, the fish was mistakenly catalogued into the invertebrate collection of the South Australian Museum, where it sat unrecognized for years.

After each chance capture the fish were preserved, then largely forgotten. The rest are held in Australian museum collections, among them the Australian Museum, Museums Victoria and CSIRO.

The whole genus is known from just seven specimens gathered over about 65 years, scattered across more than 2,500 kilometers of coastline, and nothing has been collected in nearly two decades.

The specimens are irreplaceable, so we could not dissect them. Instead we used micro-CT scanning, the same X-ray technology used in hospitals but fine enough to resolve tiny bones.

That let us build three-dimensional models of each fish’s skeleton and compare them bone by bone with true seahorses (Hippocampus).

Every earlier assessment had rested on external appearance, and the skeletons did not support it. Seahorses have a particular internal architecture, including a rigid cage of fused bony plates supporting the belly and a bony crown, called a coronet, on the head.

Our scans showed that Australyichthys has neither. In their place is a different arrangement of bones supporting the belly, one that appears in no seahorse.

A. aegis had been fixed in ethanol rather than formalin, the only member of the genus stored that way, and ethanol leaves genetic material intact. Sequencing it placed the fish well outside the seahorses, on the branch that is their closest relative. The genes said what the bones had already said.

All three species had been placed in the seahorse genus on the strength of how they look, and on that evidence they were seahorses. They are not, and they needed a genus of their own. We named it Australyichthys, from the Latin for southern and the Greek for fish.

When separate lineages evolve to look alike, biologists call it convergent evolution, and it usually reflects a shared way of life rather than shared ancestry.

The whole seahorse body, with its bent head, gripping tail and brood pouch, has been built at least twice within a single fish family, the Syngnathidae, which includes seahorses, pipefishes, pipehorses and seadragons.

Working out how that happened may reveal why evolution keeps arriving at the same solution.

All this happened along the Great Southern Reef, the connected system of kelp forests and rocky reefs that rings southern Australia. Many of its species are found nowhere else, and its deeper zones are barely explored.

In fact, an entire genus of vertebrate hid there, misidentified, until a CT scanner settled the question.

No one has ever seen one of these fish alive; they have turned up only by chance in a passing net or dredge. On that record they now qualify as lost species, known from a handful of preserved animals and never from a living one.

Calling them lost is not a prediction of extinction. It marks them as a priority for targeted surveys that go looking rather than waiting for the next accidental catch. They are most likely still down there, in a part of the sea we hardly ever visit.

#602. FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, alleging retailer overcharged shoppers

The Federal Trade Commission said Monday that it filed a lawsuit along with 20 states accusing Dollar General of charging customers more than the prices it displays on shelves, price tags and in advertisements.

Shares of Dollar General dropped about 4% after the FTC announced the lawsuit.

The complaint alleges that thousands of Dollar General stores have "taken advantage of vulnerable shoppers by extracting millions of dollars in unlawful overcharges with insufficient safeguards to prevent the practice."

It also argues that Dollar General has received "tens of thousands" of complaints from consumers about charging higher than advertised prices, but that it has not implemented policies to address the problem.

The states joining the FTC in the lawsuit are Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.

"Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last," said Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection.

Dollar General issued a statement in response to the lawsuit, saying it will "defend this litigation vigorously."

"As with other retailers and despite our policies and procedures, occasional price discrepancies can occur," the statement read. "When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement."

Dollar General's statement said that it has cooperated with the FTC's investigation since February and has produced documents, data and sworn testimony. In September, the FTC sent a draft complaint and settlement offer. The company said it had sent a monetary counteroffer and was surprised when the FTC filed the lawsuit rather than responding to the offer.

The suit comes as shoppers look for discounts while they face elevated food and gas prices. Officials across the political spectrum also aim to show their efforts to protect consumers from high costs ahead of the midterm election next week.

#600. Scientists discover a bacterial defense so strange they thought it was broken

Scientists at Gladstone Institutes have discovered an unusual bacterial immune system that operates in almost the opposite way of previously known defenses. The surprising mechanism allows bacteria to activate a deadly self-destruct process when viruses attack, potentially offering new ideas for developing medical treatments and gene-editing technologies.

The findings, published in Molecular Cell, reveal how a group of bacterial defense systems called "type VI retrons" use an unexpectedly complex sequence of molecular events to fight infection. Unlike other retrons, these systems rely on DNA to activate a toxin rather than keep one suppressed.

Understanding this unusual process could do more than expand scientists' knowledge of bacterial immunity. It may also provide a foundation for designing more effective DNA-editing tools, potentially allowing researchers to correct harmful genetic mutations with greater precision.

"This is, by far, the strangest of the retron systems that we or anyone else has come across," says Gladstone Investigator Seth Shipman, PhD, senior author of the new study. "These retrons operate with Rube Goldberg-level complexity, using molecular mechanisms that we would never have thought to invent, but that we'll use in future technologies."

How Bacteria Sacrifice Themselves to Stop Viruses

Bacteria face constant threats from viruses known as phages, which infect bacterial cells and use their machinery to reproduce. Over time, bacteria have evolved a variety of defenses to prevent these viruses from spreading.

Among these defenses are retrons, molecular systems that can detect certain viral infections and trigger the infected bacterium to destroy itself. Although this sacrifice kills the individual cell, it prevents the virus from producing more copies and infecting nearby bacteria, helping protect the larger colony.

Retrons are also of considerable interest to scientists developing new genetic technologies. They can efficiently produce and deliver single-stranded DNA, making them promising tools for editing DNA inside human cells. Shipman's team and other researchers are investigating whether these capabilities could eventually be used to correct mutations responsible for disease with exceptional accuracy.

Until now, scientists believed they understood the basic way retron defenses operate.

In previously studied retrons, a toxic protein is already present inside an uninfected cell, but its harmful effects are held in check by short pieces of single-stranded DNA. When a phage infects the bacterium, it disrupts this protective arrangement, allowing the toxin to act. The resulting cell death prevents the virus from spreading.

The newly investigated type VI retrons, however, did not appear to follow this familiar pattern.

A Bacterial Immune System That Works Backward

Researchers first became suspicious that type VI retrons were different when they could not detect the single-stranded DNA normally associated with these systems.

"The way we typically detect retrons inside uninfected cells is by looking for this single-stranded DNA," says Karen Zhang, a PhD student in Shipman's lab and lead author of the study. "But type VI retrons caught our attention because they didn't appear to have this signature. It was very odd, and we wondered if they might be broken."

Despite their unusual behavior, experiments showed that bacteria carrying type VI retrons could still defend themselves against phage infections. The systems were clearly functional, even though they lacked the expected molecular signs of activity.

"That kicked off a long molecular odyssey," Shipman says. "Whenever we tried the experiments we normally use to study retrons, they would fail, so we kept having to think of new ways to figure out how these retrons work."

After extensive investigation, the team discovered that type VI retrons reverse a key step in the usual defense process.

Rather than maintaining a substantial supply of single-stranded DNA and toxin before infection, these retrons produce little detectable DNA and no noticeable amount of toxin in healthy cells. The arrival of a phage triggers a sharp increase in DNA production.

As the DNA accumulates, it interacts with an RNA molecule that has been preventing the toxin from being made. This interaction removes the restriction, allowing the bacterium to rapidly produce the toxic protein.

The toxin appears to be an exceptionally small protein that inserts itself into the bacterium's surrounding cell membrane. By disrupting the membrane's stability, it causes the infected cell to die, stopping the viral infection from spreading.

In other words, the DNA acts as an activation switch rather than a restraint. Instead of preventing an existing toxin from causing harm, it helps turn on toxin production only when the bacterium detects a threat.

"It's almost the mirror-image version of how we traditionally view retrons, because the DNA switches on toxin production instead of inhibiting an already-produced toxin," Zhang says. "It would be fascinating to explore how bacterial evolution could have resulted in such a complex molecular system -- whether type VI retrons are older or newer than other retrons, or whether they're a stepping stone between different types."

An Unusual Discovery Required New Experiments

Figuring out how type VI retrons function proved unusually difficult. Many established techniques that scientists use to examine retrons repeatedly produced no useful results, forcing the team to develop new experimental strategies and adapt existing methods.

One particularly important challenge involved detecting the DNA produced by type VI retrons in cells that had not been infected.

After conventional tests failed, the researchers tried a technique called Spacer-seq, which had previously been developed in Shipman's laboratory. The method uses components of CRISPR-Cas, another bacterial immune system, to record molecular activity inside cells.

CRISPR-Cas is best known for its role in modern gene-editing technologies, but bacteria originally evolved these systems as defenses against viruses. Spacer-seq takes advantage of this natural machinery to help researchers investigate what happens inside cells.

The alternative approach finally revealed a trace amount of single-stranded DNA that earlier experiments had missed.

"We had just about given up hope that any DNA was being made when this approach finally revealed a very, very low level of production in uninfected cells," Zhang says.

This breakthrough encouraged the researchers to continue investigating. Additional experiments confirmed that type VI retrons produce DNA at very low levels under normal conditions and substantially increase production only after a phage enters the cell.

The findings explained why the defense system had appeared inactive in earlier tests and revealed the unusual sequence of events responsible for its antiviral activity.

Could This Strange Bacterial Defense Lead to New Medical Treatments?

The discovery is already influencing research in Shipman's laboratory, where scientists are exploring ways to transform the type VI retron's natural machinery into useful technologies.

One promising application involves developing synthetic molecular sensors and switches that can regulate gene activity. Such systems could potentially allow researchers to control when particular genes are activated or suppressed, opening new possibilities for studying disease and designing treatments.

"This system represents a unique way to potentially build a molecular sensor and switch encoded in DNA and RNA, that no one has thought of before," Zhang says. "Synthetic sensors and switches have many possible applications, both in treating disease and in designing experiments to better understand how certain diseases operate."

Another possibility involves the retron's unusually small but powerful toxins. Because these proteins can disrupt bacterial membranes and kill cells, researchers are investigating whether they could be adapted into new antimicrobial treatments.

Such therapies could potentially target harmful bacteria responsible for human infections, providing a new approach to combating bacterial disease.

These medical applications remain under development, but the discovery offers researchers a molecular design that would have been difficult to imagine without studying nature's existing solutions.

"This study highlights why it's so important for a molecular technology development lab like ours to keep looking to nature for inspiration," Shipman says. "We can use what evolution has given us as starting points to build complex machines that would have been tremendously hard to even conceptualize."

The research also raises intriguing questions about bacterial evolution, including how such an elaborate defense arose and whether type VI retrons represent an earlier, later, or intermediate stage in the evolution of these immune systems.

For scientists seeking new ways to manipulate DNA, control genes, and fight infections, this backward-acting bacterial defense could provide an unexpected starting point.

The research, "Reverse transcribed ssDNA derepresses translation of a retron antiviral protein," was published in Molecular Cell on October 13, 2026.

Along with Shipman and Zhang, the authors include Matías Rojas-Montero, Darshini Poola, and Alejandro González-Delgado of Gladstone; Josepha Klas, Arturo Carabias, Dennis Zhang, Mario Mestre, Ruiliang Zhao, Ana Dávila-Hidalgo, Guillermo Montoya, and Rafael Pinilla-Redondo of the University of Copenhagen; and Lieza Chan and Kliment Verba of UC San Francisco.

The research received support from the National Science Foundation, the Robert J. Kleeberg Jr. and Helen C. Kleberg Foundation, the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, the Lundbeck Foundation, the Fulbright U.S. Student Program, the Junta de Castilla y León and European Social Fund Plus, the European Molecular Biology Organization, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the European Research Council, and the Villum Foundation.

#599. Best Sunrise Alarm Clock (2026): Hatch, Lumie

With darker days ahead, waking up in the morning can be rough. If you never feel rested when your alarm goes off, a sunrise alarm clock could change your life. The gradually brightening light signals that it’s time to wake up instead of beeps and harsh, unnatural tones. I’m a chronic snooze-button kind of gal, and I’ve found a sunrise clock, or wake-up light, incredibly helpful for getting up when I need to and for supporting a healthier circadian rhythm. Plus, it’s much harder to ignore than a phone alarm that I can simply snooze.

If you want to face dark winter mornings by waking up more gently and naturally, using a sunrise alarm clock might just improve your mood. We recommend the newly released Hatch Sleep Clock if you want a sunrise alarm and sleep tracker in one machine, as well as a personal favorite, the Lumie Bodyclock Luxe 700FM.

Here are our favorite sunrise alarm clocks, each tested for up to a week.

Updated October 2026: We’ve added the Hatch Sleep Clock, Philips SmartSleep Wake-up Light, Rise Centered, Melalight Red Light Lamp, and pros and cons; removed the out-of-stock WiiM Wake-up Light; and ensured links and prices are up to date.

Your body is built to wake naturally with the sunrise and feel sleepy as the sun sets. The light at both the beginning and end of the day is warm and golden, unlike the bright, slightly blue midday sunlight that keeps you wide awake. A sunrise alarm clock mimics this transition from morning to bright daytime light, helping signal your body to wake up (or fall asleep, if the clock also has a sunset option).

A sunrise alarm has a built-in light you can set to brighten at a certain time. It doesn’t happen instantly; it will slowly transition over a period of anywhere from 10 minutes to an hour, and better sunrise alarms let you choose your exact brightening window. I usually choose a half-hour window for the light to start brightening, and let the gradually brightening light wake me.

There are also sound effects. Sunrise alarms feature a mix of relaxing and classic sounds that usually start when the light begins to brighten, helping to rouse you. I’d prefer the light to go first, with music activating later, but that isn’t always an option with these lights.

Some sunrise alarms also offer a sunset routine, meaning you can turn them on at night and they'll slowly dim to darkness to help you feel sleepy. It’s another good visual cue for your brain and body that it’s time for bed, and I prefer sunrise alarms like Hatch and Lumie that let you choose when to activate a routine (for example, pressing a button starts the routine over the course of 30 minutes) rather than needing to be in bed by a set time to use the routine.

Ultimately, these lights can do a lot. They can double as a sound machine, help you wake up and fall asleep, and even serve as a regular bedside lamp if they’re bright enough. Not all sunrise alarms have all of these features, though, so you have to decide how much you want to spend and which features are most important to you.

You might see a range of features listed for a sunrise alarm, and more expensive models will include more of these than cheaper models. If you’re not sure which features you want, try this series of questions to figure out which features you need.

Do you struggle to fall asleep? Splurge on a sunrise alarm with a nighttime or wind-down routine. These help establish a routine that makes it easier to fall asleep.

Do you need one device that doubles as an alarm and a bedside lamp? Get a brighter sunrise clock with easy controls to turn it on as a bedside lamp. Not all sunrise clocks have these features, so check the details carefully (and reviews like mine!) and note that cheaper, smaller sunrise alarm clocks usually won’t brighten an entire bedroom.

Are you picky about your alarm sounds? Check how many sounds are offered. Just about every sunrise clock has some sound machine features and options, but cheaper models tend to offer only a couple of sounds and might not have the sound you’re looking for.

Do you want app control? Some options in this guide don’t include a companion app or Wi-Fi capabilities, especially some of my favorites. An app doesn’t necessarily make a sunrise clock better, but it can be convenient to use. If you prefer an app to set up your sunrise lamp, try Casper, Hatch, and Loftie.

The Hatch Sleep Clock is the company’s latest sunrise alarm and its first to offer contactless sleep tracking. Priced at $249, it sits between bedside trackers like the Google Nest Hub (2nd Gen) and pricier systems like Eight Sleep. It costs as much as an Apple Watch SE 3, but you’ll get a more stripped-down picture of your sleep, without the physiological measurements or audio data you’d get from a wearable. Otherwise, it’s essentially the Restore 3 (below), doubling as a dimmable light and sound machine. You’ll need a Hatch membership ($6 per month) to unlock the audio library, but it’s worth it for the full bedtime experience. The Sleep Clock is great if you want a sunrise alarm that also functions as a sleep tracker, and/or if you’re done with strapping gadgets to your body overnight. —Boutayna Chokrane

This is my personal favorite sunrise alarm. It’s big and bright, with a stylish exterior. It has a button for lamp mode, so you can easily switch it on in the evening as a regular lamp, and it’s bright enough to fill my bedroom like a normal lamp. It has a nice range of sounds and not only connects to the radio but also allows you to save five stations. There are both sunrise and sunset settings. The biggest downside is that it only has a 24-hour clock and doesn’t connect to Wi-Fi or an app, so you have to set the time manually (and change it manually for daylight saving). If you want to spend less, the Shine 300 ($169) is a little smaller and has fewer sounds, but otherwise it’s similarly great. —Nena Farrell

The Hatch Restore 3 and its previous generations are probably the most popular sunrise alarm clocks. I constantly see the Restore 3 recommended online, from gift guides to TikTok videos, and it's understandable why it's so popular. It’s controlled by the Hatch app, which offers a wide range of sounds, lights, and routines you can use for both mornings and evenings. The Restore 3 came out in early 2025 and has more buttons and controls, so once you set up your favorite settings, you can easily toggle them on with the press of a button. The Restore 3 isn't too large, which is nice for fitting onto bedside tables, but it's not quite as bright as I'd like to force me to wake up in the morning. Note that some of Hatch’s audio content requires a Hatch+ subscription. —Nena Farrell

Casper Glow Light for $129: This light is cool because it responds to touch and movement. It turns on or off when you flip it over, and when you twist it, it brightens or dims the light. There are no sound features, but it is battery-powered and intuitive to use. —Nena Farrell

Melalight Red Light Lamp for $169: If you’re looking for something super simple, the Melalight might be what you want. This red-light lamp promises to help you wind down with its 660-nanometer wavelength. It’s the same wavelength commonly found in red-light masks to improve your skin, but it won’t impact your face from your bedside table; instead, Melalight says this wavelength is melatonin-friendly. Red- and warmer-toned lights are known to help you relax, as opposed to blue light, which is why your phone and e-readers often have a warm-light mode for evening use. You can turn it on and off by tapping the Melalight logo on the front, and adjust the brightness by holding it. There are two buttons on the back to set a 30- or 60-minute timer so it turns itself off. It’s portable and rechargeable, making it a good option if you're short on outlets at your bedside. It’s not bright enough for reading, but I’d use it with a backlit e-reader. It won’t wake you up, but it’s an option to help you fall asleep. —Nena Farrell

Blueair Mini Restful Air Purifier Sunrise Clock for $124: This device combines an air purifier with a sunrise alarm clock. The Mini Restful is the smallest air purifier in Blueair’s Sleep Collection, and it promises to gently wake you and clean the air in your bedroom. You’ll use Blueair’s app, which includes nine sounds, and you can start your sunrise anywhere from 15 to 30 minutes before your alarm. You can read more in our guide to multi-use air purifiers. —Nena Farrell

Hatch Baby for $80: The updated version of the popular Hatch Rest is the Hatch Baby, with a new look and app options similar to the Hatch Restore 3 above. (Previously, the app options were much simpler, even though the devices all share the same Hatch Sleep app.) This is a fun option for kids, though it doesn’t offer gradual sunrises. It does, however, turn on fun colors and play music at certain times and for set durations. My 3-year-old looks forward to the “green light” turning on every morning (but this does not, unfortunately, keep him from leaving his bed for mine at 4 in the morning). You’ll also get a six-month subscription to Hatch+ content. —Nena Farrell

Loftie Lamp for $280: Loftie’s lamp is gorgeous; it’s my favorite for filling my bedroom. It has three light colors and a handful of brightness settings for each. But for the high price, you need the Loftie Alarm to get sound features, and there’s only a nine-minute brightening and dimming window, which doesn’t help me much. It syncs with Alexa, though. —Nena Farrell

Rise Centered Original Sunrise Alarm Clock for $199: This unique sunrise alarm clock features a beautiful, spherical salt lamp on your choice of a beech or walnut wood base. There are no subscriptions, no Wi-Fi, and no Bluetooth, specifically to discourage phone use around bedtime. I tested the Himalayan pink salt version, but found its light to be far too dim and muted to wake me up. The company says the white version is brighter. Still, I absolutely love the look of this clock and, because it's touch-controlled, it makes an excellent bedside lamp on its own. —Kat Merck

Philips SmartSleep Wake-up Light for $109: The SmartSleep wake-up light was once our budget pick and remains one of the most basic—and least expensive—options on this list. It offers 20 brightness settings, simulated sunset and sunrise settings, five natural wake-up sounds, FM radio, tap-to-snooze, and an automatically dimming display. This basic model is best for people who want help waking up more gently but don’t need much else. —Molly Higgins

Do Sunrise Alarms Work for Heavy Sleepers?

Yes! I'm a heavy sleeper in the morning, and these can still help me wake up. You might want to choose the most gradual increase in brightness on the sunrise lamp you choose, so the slow brightening of the room can better rouse you from that deep sleep.

What’s the Difference Between a Sunrise Clock and a SAD Lamp?

These two gadgets might look similar on the outside, but sunrise clocks and other wake-up-style lights are designed to wake you up, while a SAD (seasonal affective disorder) lamp is meant to simulate sunlight during the day. SAD lamps provide light therapy to help combat seasonal depression during the darker months, while sunrise alarms are just meant to make the morning wake-up less rough. Both can help regulate your circadian rhythm, but in different ways.

How Does WIRED Choose Sunrise Clocks to Test?

We research all models in advance to determine which are a fit for testing. We ensure they have wake-up features. (Some SAD lamps look similar to a sunrise alarm, for example, but if there’s no gradual sunrise to wake up to, they don’t qualify for testing with this guide.) We also test a variety of price points and additional features to see what’s really worth buying. We make an effort to select both more affordable options with fewer features and high-end options to compare and contrast in our testing rounds.

I tested each recommended sunrise clock on my bedside table in a room with blackout curtains to see how much it could brighten the room over the course of its sunrise routine. I slept with each model for anywhere between one and seven nights, depending on its performance. I also tried out the various sound options each machine had to offer to test the speakers and see how pleasant the sounds were for waking up or falling asleep. If there was a nighttime routine option, I tested that too.
