#506. Gen Z protests in Germany: Is France-style violence looming?

Young people in Germany are preparing to protest over education and climate change. Politicians fear violence like in France, but an expert sees differences.

As politicians in Germany look ahead to the coming weekend, many fear that cities across the country could witness the kind of violent unrest that recently shook France. An initiative known as "Gen Z regelt" ("Gen Z sorts it") has launched a social media campaign calling for demonstrations in 23 cities nationwide.

"Gen Z" broadly refers to the generation born between 1995 and 2010. Many feel that their parents' generation has done too little to combat climate change and has allowed the gap between rich and poor to widen ever further. At the same time, they are concerned about their educational prospects and future opportunities.

In France, what began as largely peaceful protests recently spiraled into serious unrest. Cars were set alight in several towns, while in Limoges the town hall was torched. In Lille, Lyon, and Toulouse and elsewhere, police deployed tear gas, leading to numerous arrests.

Many politicians, particularly within Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), are warning of similar scenes this coming weekend.

Alexander Throm, the CDU parliamentary group's domestic spokesperson, told the daily Handelsblatt newspaper: "Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Throm's view, far-left groups and criminals from immigrant communities could "hijack" the demonstrations. "An ominous alliance is emerging, particularly in Berlin," he warned.

Marc Henrichmann, also of the CDU, chair of the Bundestag's parliamentary oversight panel for the intelligence services, also expressed concern: "The far-left extremist scene is internationally connected and coordinated." He said that violent far-left activists now even cross national borders to engage in looting and acts of violence elsewhere.

But Sebastian Koos, sociologist at the University of Konstanz whose research focuses on youth and protest movements, told DW that he does not expect Germany to experience unrest on a scale comparable to that seen in France, even though events in the neighboring country helped spark the protests now being planned across Germany.

Koos sees key differences between young people in the two countries. "Unlike in France, these protests are not driven by the same level of anger," he said. "They have been planned, officially registered and carefully organized. The website, in particular, places strong emphasis on peaceful protest and repeatedly stresses a non-violent approach."

At the same time, the sociologist does not rule out the possibility that extremist groups could exploit the authorized demonstrations to stir up unrest: "It is certainly very important for the police and public authorities to be well prepared."

Quentin Gärtner, 19, studies biotechnology in Heidelberg and served until November of last year as secretary-general of the Federal Student Conference, which represents around 7.5 million school students in Germany.

"What unites us is that we have run out of patience with the education system. Many young people are deeply frustrated," he told DW. "The performance of German school students continues to decline, teaching positions are constantly being cut, and in many cases school buildings have seen little or no meaningful investment for years."

For Gärtner, the discontent reflects a broader problem with parliamentary democracy in Germany and many other Western countries.

"Politicians want to win elections. They focus on the groups that matter most to them electorally rather than on the future and the long-term sustainability of their policies," he said.

"And in our aging societies, older people and the baby boomer generation are the groups that carry the most political weight."

Opposition parties in Germany have also voiced understanding for the concerns of younger people. Speaking to Germany's public broadcaster ZDF, Green Party co-leader Felix Banaszak said: "The intergenerational contract is no longer working. Older generations have driven the climate into a dead end."

He argued that the social welfare system was also reaching its limits and that rents had become unaffordable. According to Banaszak, the only thing the state seems to offer young people are the letters sent to 18-year-olds asking them to consider joining the military. Germany is currently desperate to expand the Bundeswehr and is considering reintroducing national service.

By Tuesday, around 134,000 people had registered on the "Gen Z regelt" website to take part in the protests planned for the coming Saturday. With several days still to go before the demonstrations, that number could rise further.

#504. The Hollywood Color Nerd Who Shot ‘Knives Out’ Explains His Viral iPhone Camera App

Steve Yedlin is a certified color nerd. He almost immediately starts explaining “the math” behind his passion for color science.

But I didn’t call to chat about psychophysics or color theory. I called to talk to Yedlin about his Chromagraph Camera app, newly released, virally popular, and available only on the iPhone.

Yedlin is a longtime collaborator with director Rian Johnson, shooting his films like Knives Out and Star Wars: The Last Jedi. The duo teamed up again for this launch. “I write all of my own image processing that we use on the movies,” he says. The Chromagraph Camera app brings a taste of Yedlin’s special sauce to your smartphone camera.

Instead of the iPhone’s built-in image processing, this app shoots RAW image data and processes it with a similar formula to what he uses in film production. After Johnson promoted Chromagraph Camera on social media in late October, it quickly became the top paid download in the iOS store. The app costs a one-time fee of $13 and only shoots still photos. (There’s no video support yet.)

I am far from the resident photography nerd on WIRED’s gear team. (That award goes, in part, to my wonderful editor, Julian.) I’m often just whipping out my iPhone and snapping a picture with the default settings. Even so, I really enjoyed capturing some of San Francisco’s fall vibes using the Chromagraph Camera. Although Apple gives iPhone owners plenty of built-in tools for adjusting the color on your own images, I loved this app’s ability to capture highly stylized shots without me needing to fiddle with anything at all.

When you open the app, what you see in the viewfinder before snapping the shot is not what the Chromagraph Camera will spit out. The photo is essentially “developed” in the app after you capture the image. This is because the app needs a moment to run its unique processing for the specific tone, color, and grain effects. You can also alter how an image looks in the app after it’s processed, if you want to tweak the overall exposure or texture of an image.

Yedlin is adamant that he’s not attempting to replace your iPhone camera app or release a professional tool for editing everything. It’s all about that color, man. “It's just this curated app that takes the pictures the way we like,” he says. Yedlin and Johnson teamed up with programmer Eric Cameron to build the app centered around their color tastes, experimenting with it for a couple of months before launch.

Even after all of this custom image processing, Yedlin still sees the iPhone as a fundamentally limited device. “This idea that you can actually have the control that a professional camera would have is not really true anyhow,” he says. Software can only do so much to change how hardware works, especially when developing an app within Apple’s parameters that limit how far the software can push the phone’s hardware.

As advances in computational photography and generative AI have renewed discussions about what a smartphone photo even is anymore, Yedlin’s approach isn’t an attempt to find a sense of neutrality. He doesn’t see any image as a literal rendering of what exists. It’s always an interpretation, whether that’s a stylized, artful depiction or a more stagnant shot. He says that the look of the Chromagraph Camera app is consciously “opinionated” and specific.

“You can describe how the different rendering looks in words, but you just have to look at it,” he says. The color speaks for itself.

#503. NASA reaches out to commercial space industry for help saving legendary Hubble Space Telescope

Sad news for space aficionados: the famous Hubble Space Telescope, responsible for some of the most jaw-dropping images of our solar system taken more than three decades since its launch into low-Earth orbit in 1990, is on a slow path towards a fiery fate. At its present rate of altitude loss, NASA's most famous telescope is expected to re-enter Earth's atmosphere sometime in 2033 or 2034, at which point it will come crashing down like a comet, according to Space.com, possibly endangering human life on its descent

It doesn't have to be that way, though. If NASA had more room in its budget, it could repeat its 2002 Space Shuttle Columbia mission STS-109 and give the aging telescope a nudge into a higher orbit, extending its lifespan. In desperation, NASA has put out a Request for Information (RFI) to the fast-growing commercial space sector, hoping for aid to either boost Hubble's altitude and extend its lifespan or else guide its descent to a safe crash site, such as the middle of the ocean.

According to the RFI, a successful orbital boost would require an ascent of more than 370 miles (600 kilometers), which is a significant increase in elevation and an astonishingly difficult challenge from a purely technical perspective.

In a statement on the NASA website, Nicky Fox, an associate administrator of the Science Mission Directorate, spoke to the growing power and influence of the private space sector: "Commercial industry has rapidly evolved in recent years to offer new capabilities for in-space satellite capture and servicing. Given the time we have until Hubble’s anticipated re-entry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow."

NASA administrator Jared Isaacman spoke of a duty to both "the American taxpayer" and "the scientific community" to explore all possible ways to extend Hubble's life, and the project is likely to attract serious interest from companies like Elon Musk's SpaceX and Peter Beck's Rocket Lab, which became famous for successfully catching a used rocket with a helicopter.

It wouldn't even be the first time that the commercial space sector has lent NASA a helping hand. In March of last year, stranded astronauts Suni Williams and Butch Wilmore were rescued from the International Space Station with assistance from SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft.

Let's hope history repeats itself and NASA finds a willing collaborator, because Hubble's insights over more than a three decades have radically altered our understanding of the universe we inhabit and inspired new generations to look to the stars.

#502. Restaurant Brands reports mixed results as Burger King's U.S. turnaround shows signs of success

Restaurant Brands International on Thursday reported mixed quarterly results as Popeyes' struggles offset Burger King's successful U.S. turnaround.

Shares of the company fell about 2% in morning trading.

Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Restaurant Brands reported third-quarter net income attributable to common shareholders of $542 million, or $1.54 per share, up from $315 million, or 96 cents per share, a year earlier.

Excluding certain noncash items, the company earned $1.10 per share.

Across all of its restaurants, the company reported same-store sales growth of 3.8%. Restaurant Brands has reported same-store sales growth above 3% for the past five quarters.

While the broader industry saw traffic soften in the third quarter as gas prices stayed high, Restaurant Brands said it has not seen any significant changes in consumer behavior.

"The environment, from what we see, has been relatively stable over the last couple of quarters and even into recent months," Restaurant Brands CEO Josh Kobza told CNBC.

Burger King was the top performer, with U.S. same-store sales growth of 8.4%. The burger chain's home market is in the middle of multiyear turnaround, with a focus on improving its food and restaurants.

"The plans we've put in place over the last several years are working, and we're going to keep executing against them," Restaurant Brands Chair Patrick Doyle said on the company's earnings conference call. "Burger King has delivered over four years of industry outperformance, and now we've seen three consecutive quarters of truly exceptional results."

After improving the quality of its Whopper earlier this year, Burger King turned its attention to its nuggets and sauces.

"Nuggets and sauces, frankly, we knew for a while that there was an opportunity," Kobza told CNBC. "We've heard it loud and clear from our guests."

Since Burger King relaunched its nuggets on Sept. 1, with 100% white meat chicken, sales have shot up more than 35%, Kobza said on the earnings call. More core menu items will get an upgrade next year.

Tim Hortons reported same-store sales growth of 1.8% in Canada, its home market. In July, the coffee chain launched a line of matcha drinks, bringing more customers to its locations during the sleepier afternoon hours.

Popeyes was once again the laggard of Restaurant Brands' portfolio. The fried chicken chain's U.S. same-store sales fell 2.2%.

In recent quarters, Popeyes has struggled as other chicken rivals have lured its customers away with discounts. Restaurant Brands is trying to stage a comeback with improved restaurant operations and a focus on its core menu.

Restaurant Brands previously forecast that Popeyes would return to same-store sales growth in the second half of 2026, but Kobza said on the earnings call that the company now believes it will take longer, although traffic is improving. The return of Popeyes' $6 Big Box promotion in September boosted sales less than expected, according to Kobza. Plus, the chain has scaled back its wings to refocus on its core menu items, hurting sales in the short term.

The company's international business saw same-store sales growth of 3.9%, fueled by its Burger King locations.

#500. Evacuation from Oleshky: How are preparations going?

A lawyer with the Save Ukraine Foundation, Myroslava Kharchenko, told DW about what has been happening in Russian-occupied Oleshky since a temporary ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump took effect.

Since a ceasefire took effect in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region on October 27, preparations have been underway to evacuate residents trapped there.

Following Russia's occupation of the town in 2022 and the flooding caused by the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka dam in 2023, residents were cut off from the outside world. All access routes to Oleshky, which lies on the Dnipro River, had been mined. Former Oleshky residents who managed to escape and talked to DW described hunger, no access to medicine, and no electricity or water. About 2,000 people are still living in the town.

According to the Save Ukraine Foundation, it has rescued at least 300 civilians from Oleshky over the past six months. DW spoke with lawyer Myroslava Kharchenko, who works for the organization, about preparations for the upcoming evacuation.

DW: A ceasefire is already in effect in Oleshky. Do you know whether any evacuation efforts have begun?

Myroslava Kharchenko: No, we do not have that information yet. What we do know is that the ceasefire came into effect on October 27 at 3 a.m. Kyiv time, which is 4 a.m. in Russia. Mine-clearing operations on the road began at around 8 a.m. What is happening inside Oleshky itself, however, is entirely within the military's remit. Everyone involved in this operation has been asked to maintain strict confidentiality. Any careless remark or action could jeopardize the entire evacuation effort.

What I can see is that information is being actively collected through closed internal local chat groups. Registration lists and application forms are being shared, and people are filling them out themselves. Organizers are contacting those who previously requested evacuation to verify details such as their date of birth and current place of residence. They are also asking people to provide contact information for neighbors or relatives who may be nearby or in the same building, because communications are extremely unreliable.

The organizers are also collecting information about the health conditions of those planning to leave. Among them are people who are ill, have limited mobility, or are recovering from recent injuries, including blast and mine-related wounds. We therefore expect those organizing the evacuation to ensure that medical assistance is available for those who need it.

How exactly is the evacuation expected to take place? Will people be evacuated through Russian-controlled territory or via the Dnipro River? Have any routes already been agreed upon?

As far as we know, a river route would be extremely dangerous. We have not heard any confirmation that such an option has been approved. It therefore appears likely that the evacuation route will pass through the temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory and possibly through Russia before people are able to reach Ukraine. For security reasons, however, none of these details are being made public.

What do you know about the number of people expected to be evacuated?

We are actually very pleased that the evacuation is not expected to take place in a single day. That is important because we hope that those who manage to leave safely during the first stage will serve as an example for others.

People still trapped in Oleshky are extremely afraid. There have already been numerous provocations, and this is not the first attempt to establish such a route or humanitarian corridor.

As a result, there is a great deal of suspicion. Those concerns are based largely on uncertainty, and some people may choose not to leave during the initial phase of the evacuation. Overall, however, we estimate that around 500 people may eventually be evacuated.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How would you assess the role of Melania Trump in making this evacuation possible?

We are immensely grateful to Melania Trump for drawing attention to the humanitarian catastrophe currently unfolding in Oleshky. What is taking place there is in fact genocide committed by the Russian Federation.

We are thankful for her efforts and hope they will help make this evacuation possible. We will be even more grateful once most people are safely removed from the combat zone and arrive in Ukrainian government-controlled territory.

When could the physical evacuation of civilians begin?

I can't say how long it will take. What seems clear, however, is that time will be needed to clear mines from the roads leading into the city. We also understand that many streets inside Oleshky are mined, so additional work will be required to make routes within the city safe.

There is a hospital from which people need to be evacuated. Nearby is a morgue where bodies also need to be recovered.

I do not know whether that will be included as part of this humanitarian corridor, but it is undoubtedly important. The bodies need to be identified and the causes of death established. That process will also take time, regardless of how quickly the military is able to work.

It is difficult to make any predictions because, as you can see, everything is being conducted under strict secrecy. Statements from both the Russian and Ukrainian sides have been extremely cautious, and that is clearly justified under the circumstances.

#499. There’s a Free Video Editor Inside Google Drive That Anyone Can Use

Mention the online apps available as part of Google Workspace, and most people will immediately think of Google Drive, Gmail, Google Docs, Google Sheets, and Google Slides—those speedy, lightweight office apps that let you get work done from any browser tab.

There's more to the suite of Google Workspace tools than you might have realized though, including an online video editing package called Google Vids. Originally launched in 2024 for business and enterprise users, the app was made available to individuals in 2026 and continues to get regular updates from Google.

Since it's both free to use and designed to run in a web browser, it's not capable of pro-level, high-resolution, multitrack video editing. But for personal and hobbyist use, it works well, and it won't take you long to learn the basics.

Finding Google Vids isn't difficult: You can either open Google Drive on the web, then click New and Google Vids, or head straight to the Google Vids app page and click the + (plus) button under Start a new video. (Any videos you've previously made are shown here, too.)

Besides beginning with a clean state (the Blank vid option), there are plenty of other ways to get started: You can generate AI videos with the Veo 3.1 model, turn a slideshow into a video, work from a template, upload an existing video as a starting point, create an AI music track, record a video using your camera, produce a video with an AI avatar, or create a storyboard outline. Note you can also pick the video orientation at the top.

Most of these options use a similar layout, and we're going to focus on the traditional video-making approach here—though the AI options are well worth exploring, too, if you don't have source material to work with. If you're new to Google Vids, then picking Templates from the opening splash screen will ease you in gently.

When it comes to picking a template, the topic isn't as important as the layout. Look for something that matches what you want to create as closely as possible (hover over any of the thumbnails to see an animated preview). The next dialog lets you choose whether you want to use the entire template or just selected scenes. After that, you're into the video editing interface proper.

Most of the elements should be relatively familiar if you've ever used a timeline-based video editor in the past. At the bottom you've got your video and audio tracks, while the main window shows the currently selected segment of your video. The panel on the right lets you edit whatever's currently selected.

Down the right side of the interface you've got all the options for loading in new content. You can record webcam clips, create AI videos, import footage from Google Drive and Google Photos, add voiceovers, and drop in text, images, music, and shapes. If you've started with a template, some of these elements will be styled to match.

Along the top of the Google Vids interface are more editing and formatting tools. These menus are where you should head to change transitions between scenes, to manage how elements are arranged in a particular scene, to drop in new scenes, and to manage your video project as a whole.

To begin building your projects, you'll probably want to load in audio, video, and images via the buttons on the right. On the most basic level, you can click the + (plus) button on the timeline to create a new scene, then drag in a photo or video from the right-hand panel to fill the scene you've just created.

A whole host of options present themselves when you right-click on the timeline. You can, for example, mute the audio track imported with a video, then add a voiceover or some different music. You're also able to split scenes (if you only want to keep half a scene maybe) and duplicate scenes (for quickly expanding the running time of your project) with a right-click.

Keep your eye on the panel on the right, which changes depending on the context. With audio tracks, you can apply fades, and with video clips you can choose from different transitions. If your scene has several elements (like shapes that scroll over a video), you're able to adjust how they look and behave.

Let's say you have a video scene and want to put some text over it. Select the scene in the timeline, click the Text button on the right, then click Add a title to do just that. If you then select the title in the scene itself, you can change the text and its styling.

Using the handles around the text box you can change its position, size, and rotation. There are also three buttons underneath on a floating toolbar: Animation lets you animate the text, Resize will resize the text box to fit the text you've entered, and Format options brings up a panel where you can change text size, padding, rotation, and so on.

Click and drag on elements inside a scene to reposition them, and right-click for more options—including Cut, Copy, Paste, and Delete. If you need more material to work with, choose the Stock option on the right, which gives you a library of material you can make use of in addition to your own content and anything created with AI.

There's a lot more to Google Vids, but that should be enough to get you started—try experimenting with a few of the templates to see what else is possible. As with the other Google Drive apps, all your edits are saved instantly, and up in the top right corner you've got a Play button for viewing your work in progress, and a Share button for when it’s ready for the world to see.

#496. The 30 Best Gifts for Star Wars Fans (2026)

I have received many, many Star Wars gifts over the years. I spent the first Christmas Day that I can remember flying Luke and his X-wing around the house. I met Darth Vader (David Prowse) when I was 6. I can still feel the shiver of fear as he strode through the double doors, reaching over the crowd to shake hands with me as my dad held me up. I never questioned why the Dark Lord of the Sith was in Woolworth’s.

When I became a dad, I had a fresh excuse to visit that galaxy far, far away and buy new toys. (I still regret selling my own in a garage sale to raise funds for our first home.) My wife and I love the original movies, and our kids prefer the prequel trilogy, but we all enjoyed watching the latest shows together. And because just about everyone knows I’m a fan, I have received (and given) countless Star Wars gifts over the years. These are some of my favorites.

For more recommendations, check out my picks for The Best Gifts for Lego Fans, Best STEM Gifts for Kids, and Best Gifts Under $25.

Updated November 2026: I added a marble run, a jigsaw puzzle, and an advent calendar. I also updated prices throughout.

Hasbro’s Black Series of Star Wars helmets strikes the right balance between quality and price. They look good enough to satisfy collectors but come cheaper than high-end movie replicas. My favorite is the sadly discontinued original battered Boba Fett helmet. You can still find it or the newer re-armored version if you're prepared to pay an inflated bounty. Many other Black Series helmets, including Vader and various Troopers, are also excellent and still available.

I have spent many hours building Star Wars Lego sets with my kids, and nothing compares to the Death Star (if you’re looking to push the boat out), but you may also want to check out one of the new Smart Brick sets. While it’s not perfect and lacks authentic Star Wars sound effects, I did have fun with the Star Wars Smart Play Throne Room Duel and A-Wing set. Recreating the iconic final light saber battle in Star Wars: Return of the Jedi, as Emperor Palpatine sits on his throne, watching Darth Vader and Luke Skywalker fight, with light saber swooshes as a synth version of “The Imperial March” plays, will put a smile on any fan’s face.

If the Star Wars fan in your life also enjoys darts, you’ve just hit the mother lode. Target Darts has a Star Wars-themed line, and my top pick is this stylish set of Darth Vader darts. These tungsten steel-tipped beauties come in three weights with molded grippy barrels and black imperial flights. The zippy Darth case contains a spare set of red flights and tools. You can also get Darth Maul, Stormtrooper, and R2-D2-themed cases and flights, and Target Darts just released new themed sets of Mandalorian ($380) and AT-AT ($170) darts, and Grogu ($55) and Mandalorian ($55) cases. And don’t forget the Star Wars Millennium Falcon Surround and Dartboard ($200), which I tested with Target's Omni Auto Scoring System.

If you’re unfamiliar, Displates are metallic artworks with a clever magnetic mount system that makes it quick and easy to switch your prints when you want a change. The artwork is layered and textured with gloss varnish on the details, and this one, released for the 20th anniversary of Revenge of the Sith, depicts Darth, flanked by Clone Troopers, with Anakin and Obi-Wan duelling on Mustafar in the foreground. If you don’t like this particular print, Displate has an enormous Star Wars section to browse.

Any aspiring Jedi or Sith needs a lightsaber. If you want a high-quality replica that’s right for you, be prepared to research. I tried a Combat Saber from Padawan Outpost, Model Vader E6 (Xenopixel), inspired by Darth’s lightsaber from Episode VI: Return of the Jedi. There is a learning curve, but this lightsaber really looks and feels the part. You can change the color, trigger countless sound effects, and even play music. There’s also an app, so you can connect to the saber from your phone and tweak the settings. No worries if you’re not a fan of Vader, because the Outpost offers a wide range of realistic lightsabers (check here if you’re in the UK) based on those wielded in the movies and shows by everyone from Obi-Wan to Count Dooku.

WIRED readers can get a 5 percent discount with the code WIRED5.

Marble runs are universally popular with kids (mine loved them when they were younger), and this Star Wars–themed one is part of the GraviTrax series. Kids can get creative when they construct it, building different types of runs with X-Wings, Tie Fighters, a Star Destroyer, and the Millennium Falcon—all on a Death Star board. They can also potentially connect it to other GraviTrax sets.

I spent an entire summer as a kid in an Atari Star Wars cockpit cabin at my local arcade, reliving the climax of the movie in wire-frame form as I blasted TIE Fighters, sped through the Death Star trench, and timed proton torpedoes to blow it up. That 1983 release is bundled with The Empire Strikes Back (1985) and Return of the Jedi (1984) games in this ROTJ-styled arcade cabinet. It takes some building and feels a little cheap, but it does include the original yoke flight controls, and it’s still very fun to play. Just make sure your giftee has room for it, as it’s 61.5 inches tall, 19 inches wide, and 24 inches deep.

My wife and kids have been using Casetify cases with a mix of iPhones and Pixels for over a year, and we find them durable and protective, if a little chunky. Unfortunately, it’s not just the Star Wars designs that are on the dark side; these cases are also pricey.

Of the many excellent books about Star Wars, this might be my favorite. It charts the rise of the franchise, offers countless nuggets of trivia, and acknowledges the role fans have played in making Star Wars so special. It's an entertaining peek behind the scenes that is affectionate but also dares to be critical. Perhaps mercifully, it ends with the new trilogy still on the horizon.

It’s way too easy to get messy when cooking, which is why aprons exist. Respected apron purveyor Hedley & Bennett makes some top-quality aprons, and it has a Star Wars line. I tried the Darth Vader Essential Apron (a great gift for dads), and my wife tried the Ahsoka Tano Crossback Apron. We love them. The thoughtful designs include lots of wee Star Wars character references (there are eight options). Mine has an adjustable neck strap, while the Crossback goes over your shoulders. Kenner sold over 300 million Star Wars action figures in the late ’70s and early ’80s. I spent every penny of my pocket money on them for years, and there’s a roaring trade in secondhand figures. When Hasbro realized its potential, it started making new figures under the Kenner brand, and there are three main lines today. The Retro Collection is all 3.75-inch figures like the originals Kenner sold, with a peg hole in the bottom of their feet and legs that don’t bend. The Vintage Collection figures are the same size but with more detail and bendable limbs. The Black Series figures are larger, at around 6 inches tall, and tend to be much more detailed.

One of mine took a tumble and broke both his legs, but after a quick superglue treatment, he made a full recovery. I advise putting them out of reach of young kids and cats.

It’s a fun activity for fans of any age, but expect to take a few days assembling it. The finished jigsaw is huge, measuring 39 x 30 inches, so make sure you've got a proper table for the job.

#492. Hundreds of Mundane AI Apps Are Hiding Sexually Abusive Deepfake Features

At first glance, the self-proclaimed “pet portrait” app Viefur appears to be just another AI slop generator. Using digital coins sold in the app—around $4 will buy 130 coins—pet photos can be turned into an “anthropomorphic portrait,” with the critter dressed in “human clothing” and inserted into bizarre scenes. Think a hamster wearing beach shorts, sunglasses, and lounging in a swimming pool or a Hawaiian shirt-wearing cat, drinking from a coconut.

All of this is cover for what appears to be the app’s true purpose: creating sexually abusive deepfake images.

A WIRED investigation found the app is part of a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps that, like Viefur, often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.

The network was discovered hiding in plain sight, by multiple researchers, after they investigated links from thousands of video ads containing explicit deepfake content that were published on Meta’s Facebook and Instagram. As WIRED has reported in recent months, hundreds of these ads contained AI generated child sexual abuse material, including images of real children and a member of a European royal family. The ads reached tens of thousands of people and have prompted investigations from regulators around the world.

In each case, the ads linked out to the deceptive apps in Apple and Google’s app stores—allowing people to generate explicit images and make payments using Apple and Google Pay. The network behind the nudify apps appears to have been publishing them for around a year, at times publishing dozens per week. This is despite Google, Apple, and Meta saying they enforce their policies that do not allow harmful deepfake content on their platforms.

The apps and domains investigated by WIRED appear to be run by Chinese developers and a Hong Kong registered entity called KeLing Technology Limited, according to a review of web domains and how the services operate. Email addresses linked to the entity, apps, and related services, did not respond to multiple requests for comment from WIRED, but after being contacted, they appeared to erase public connections between KeLing Technology Limited and the deepfake tools.

“This is an organized, commercially run operation: One operator behind hundreds of disposable apps and domains, cloaked to pass App Store review and pushed through tens of thousands of Meta ads under fake payer names,” says Paul Bouchaud, a lead researcher at the nonprofit AI Forensics, who investigated the network. “They don’t expect enforcement to catch up, and so far it hasn’t.”

Download one of the apps in the deepfake network and you may see exactly what was advertised—such as an app to create AI pet pictures. But behind the scenes, researchers found, the apps are quietly making determinations about whether to show the benign content or load a web interface showing explicit deepfakes.

“Each time the application is downloaded, there is a call to the server with some information, such as where the user is coming from, the language, some unique identifier, and then the server replies whether or not to show the explicit or the non-explicit version of it,” explains Bouchaud, who reverse engineered the apps’ and associated websites’ code. They say there’s no clear list of reasons why one user may be shown the explicit version of an app, but one trigger appears to be downloading it after clicking an associated ad on Meta’s platforms.

Websites linked to the apps have revealed the network’s secrets and the scale that it operates on. Opening one of the apps’ websites will likely show an entirely black screen and no content. The only noticeable change is that the URL updates to include the word “risk.” But the websites host the hidden explicit deepfake layer that can be loaded in each app.

This web interface contains dozens of pornography deepfake video and image templates—with users able to upload images of people to be added to the sexual scenes. The interface allows the purchase of “diamonds” to generate images and links to other social media accounts where users can contact the developers with questions or complaints.

Also hidden in the websites’ code are details about the entire network. A JavaScript bundle that can easily be unpicked, researchers say, contains a list of all the domains and apps that have been created by the developers—including app package details, encryption keys, Facebook advertising trackers, and more.

“They contained this giant configuration list of other domains with different encryption keys,” says Maël Le Touz, a staff threat researcher at security firm Infoblox, who identified almost 500 linked domains. “They run the same code and they all reference one another.”

Bouchard’s analysis of when domains were registered found that the apps started to appear toward the end of 2025, with a spike during the spring of this year. At one point, around 30 nudify apps-websites were being registered each week, the researcher says, with 27 live on Google’s Play Store in September. These apps had been downloaded more than 350,000 times collectively and many were rated suitable for all age groups, Bouchard’s research says.

One of the most popular apps, called DiffAI, was created in December 2025 and has been downloaded more than 100,000 times from the Play Store. A user review on Google’s Play Store stated: “This app contains templates for creating CSAM and other types of pornographic material. It performs no age verification.”

DiffAI was removed from the Play Store shortly before WIRED contacted Google about the network. Google did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment, though it had removed the majority of the apps ahead of being contacted. (Portions of the deepfake network were reported on by Danish journalists in September.)

Similarly, Apple removed 19 apps from its App Store, including pet photo app Viefur, after WIRED asked the company about the activity and shared associated domains. “We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for our users, and nudification apps and other pornographic content are strictly prohibited,” says Apple spokesperson Adam Dema.

“We review every app before it’s published, and these apps complied with our rules when we reviewed them,” Dema says. “After approval, their developers changed the website the app pulls its content from, replacing what we approved with pornographic content, and promoted it through pornographic ads hosted on a third-party platform.” The company says it has suspended tens of thousands of apps for using these “bait-and-switch” tactics over the last year and recently updated its app store rules to further restrict “nudify” tools.

Central to the “nudify” network appears to be a host of Chinese developers whose identities seem to have been intentionally hidden. “It’s using exclusive Chinese hosting, the code is written in Chinese and has a lot of comments in Chinese,” Le Touz says, noting explicit videos in ads posted to Meta’s platforms promoting the apps contained watermarks from Chinese-language video editing software.

“These ads violate not just one, but several of Meta’s policies,” says Katie Paul, the director of the Tech Transparency Project, who first uncovered the ads showing deepfake explicit depictions of minors. “There is no question about what you are seeing, what the app is advertising,” she says. Paul says tech companies need to answer questions about where money generated from the apps goes and how those behind the nudification apps and services constantly seem to bypass their content moderation and safety systems.

KeLing Technology Limited appears to be a significant part of the operation. While the company’s website is little more than a shell, its name was listed as the contact details of the first website registered in the network. This website’s brand name also appeared as part of the contact details within the explicit deepfake template that was used in the apps. Bouchaud also identified an administration login page linked to the explicit deepfake interface that mentions “Keling.” And email addresses using the company’s domain appeared on at least one app that have been removed from app stores.

Towards the end of September, a notification sent to users of the explicit deepfake interface announced that a new AI model could be used—the model was called Veyra, with a tagline in the apps of “More real. More natural. More wild.” The homepage of a website called Veyra AI listed its contact email as a KeLing Technology address.

Meta says it banned KeLing Technology Limited from advertising in 2025 after it failed to “comply with a cease and desist letter.” (Meta declined to share the letter with WIRED citing legal reasons.) “We have strict rules against promoting nudify apps and work aggressively to keep this material off our services,” a Meta spokesperson says. Meta says that while KeLing Technology Limited has continued to try and advertise through other ways, it takes action against the ads when it becomes aware of them.

After WIRED shared the 400-plus domains with Meta, the spokesperson said they had shared more than 3,000 associated ads linked to them, two-thirds of which it had already removed from its systems. Meta later told WIRED it has taken action against 11,600 ad accounts, more than 4,700 business pages, 5,200 users, and 15,000 pages linked to the domains, blocking 209 apps from advertising on its platforms.

“The criminals behind them take increasingly deceptive steps to evade detection—hiding behind fake names and identities, running ads that look benign, and sometimes linking to Google's and Apple's app stores, with the ads' true intent revealed only after a click,” the spokesperson says.

As WIRED finished reporting this story, similar ads and apps continued to be published on the tech platforms.

Connections is the one of the most popular New York Times word games that's captured the public's attention. The game is all about finding the "common threads between words." And just like Wordle, Connections resets after midnight and each new set of words gets trickier and trickier—so we've served up some hints and tips to get you over the hurdle.

If you just want to be told today's puzzle, you can jump to the end of this article for today's Connections solution. But if you'd rather solve it yourself, keep reading for some clues, tips, and strategies to assist you.

The NYT's latest daily word game has become a social media hit. The Times credits associate puzzle editor Wyna Liu with helping to create the new word game and bringing it to the publications' Games section. Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

Each puzzle features 16 words and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise of anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

If a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake—players get up to four mistakes until the game ends.

Players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

#487. Norwegian shares surge 13% on earnings beat, guidance raise

Shares of Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings surged 13% Thursday after the company posted better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and raised its outlook for the full year.

The cruise line reported third-quarter revenue of $2.95 billion, topping Wall Street expectations of $2.88 billion, according to analyst estimates from LSEG.

Net income for the period was $491 million, or $1.07 per share.

Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was $937 million, which exceeded Norwegian's previous guidance of $874 million. Adjusted EPS was $1.12, exceeding previous guidance of 90 cents and outpacing analysts' expectations of 94 cents, per LSEG.

Norwegian also raised its full-year guidance, citing its stronger-than-expected third-quarter performance. The company now expects 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $2.55 billion and adjusted EPS of about $1.70.

The report said the company's bookings had "improved modestly" since its last report but remain below its optimal range.

Norwegian said it will emphasize new marketing strategies, including the launch of a new marketing platform in January. It also said it anticipates that enhancements such as a new waterpark at its Great Stirrup Cay private island will support stronger demand.

Also on Thursday, Norwegian announced that Chief Financial Officer Mark Kempa will step down after more than 25 years at the company. Meghan Montana, currently chief strategy officer, will take over the role starting Jan. 1.

#486. 4 Best Alexa Speakers I’ve Tested (2026)

Amazon started the smart speaker game, but finding the best Alexa speaker has only gotten harder as the company launches more and more devices. Amazon has the largest range of smart speakers and displays by a long shot, which can be overwhelming to dive into. It currently includes the Echo Dot Max, the Echo Studio (2nd Gen), the Echo Show 11, and the Echo Show 8 (4th Gen). But Amazon has plenty of older, cheaper models available, too.

If you're looking for something small and simple to control your home, either an Echo Dot ($80) or the Echo Dot Max ($120) is your best bet. The Dot Max has really impressive sound for its compact size and is my overall favorite Alexa speaker, but if you're only going to use it for voice commands rather than jam sessions, you can get away with the older, cheaper model, especially if you want to buy a few to place around your home. For anyone looking for a smart display, the Echo Show 11 ($250) is the best of Amazon's newest smart displays that come designed for Amazon’s updated assistant, Alexa+. The older third-generation Echo Show 8 ($150) is still a great value if you want something cheaper.

However, there are several new models out after Amazon's announcement on October 28, and I'll be updating this guide soon on whether the newest models outpace the old. In the meantime, read on to see which of the existing Echo speakers are our favorites. You can also learn more about Alexa+, and we've got guides on setting up your Echo speaker, creating Alexa routines, and the best tricks an Echo Show can do.

Updated November 2026: I've updated this guide with details about the new Echo speaker models announced, and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

Out of all of Amazon's latest smart speakers, one landed on top for me: the Echo Dot Max. It's still a similarly sized speaker to past Dot models (though this model is slightly taller at 4.27 inches while the older one was 3.9 inches), but it has much better sound than ever before, putting it on a level with the Echo (4th Gen) we previously recommended. I was really impressed with the sound quality and volume for such a small speaker. It also doesn't lack in bass like smaller speakers usually do. Amazon is no longer selling the plain Echo, which was last updated in 2020, so the Echo Dot Max is really your only powerful sound option that isn't upward of $150.

While it still has the rounded design that was introduced in the 2020 Echo speakers, both the Echo Dot Max and new Echo Studio introduced a new design style with a front panel that looks like a dust cap, but instead houses the volume controls and the microphone mute button. There are also tap controls on the top to stop music, and it has a built-in smart home hub that was never before available in such a small speaker. It comes with Alexa+ right out of the box, but if you don't have a Prime membership, you'll only have a 30-day trial and then need to pay for either Prime or the Alexa+ $20 monthly fee (choose Prime).

The price on this model also rose recently, going from a base price of $100 to $120. It's not a huge increase, but a bummer to see, especially because that means sales on this device will also likely be on the higher end than in the past. It's on sale right now for $95, for example, but that's only $5 cheaper than the price it had just a week ago.

The fifth-generation Echo Dot is a few years old now, but it's still a great little speaker. It's got powerful, robust sound for its size, and it works great if you want Alexa handy on a bookshelf or on a small side table. It's got significantly improved bass from older models, which I really like for listening to music. It's one I always find myself setting up somewhere in my house, whether it's in my hallway so I can ask quick questions as I move through the house, or in my bedroom as an alarm clock.

It used to have some of the best sound you can get for the price, but Amazon did unfortunately raise the price on this speaker along with several other models. The base price used to be $50 and frequently on sale for around $30, but the base price is now $80 with its sale price going for $55. I wouldn't buy it if it's not on sale; it's not worth $80. Still, it's the best Amazon's got in the under-$100 category after the price hikes.

★ New 2026 Model: There's a new 6th-gen Echo Dot out, but it costs $100 now since it includes a smart home hub, Omnisense to sense the environment, the ability to extend your eero mesh Wi-Fi system, and improved bass. I'll be testing it soon, but while the new features are cool, it's frustrating to see the cheaper Echos get more and more expensive.

I'm surprised to say that out of Amazon's two newest Echo Show devices, the new Echo Show 11 ended up being my favorite over the fourth-gen Echo Show 8. I actually liked the larger screen, and it didn't feel ridiculously large like the Echo Show 15 does or the Echo Show 10 before it, but it helps that the base is much smaller on the Show 11 than the Show 10's rotating, Wall-E-esque base.

The Echo Show 11's screen is bright and crisp, and I loved how the landscape photo slideshows looked on it. There's a little side menu you can swipe to see things like your smart home favorites, and I found the sound quality immersive and more well-rounded than the new Show 8. Taylor Swift's “You're On Your Own, Kid” sounded beautifully dimensional, while “Opalite” didn't lose its bass like it did on the newer Show 8. It's got a 13-MP camera like we've seen on Show 8 models, and this larger display is one I'd be more likely to stream a show on compared to the smaller Show 8 and Show 5 sizes. If you're looking to get one of the newer displays, this is the superior option.

This smart display also rose in price due to Amazon's price hikes. It now has a base price of $250, when it used to be $220.

The Echo Show 8 has been our favorite smart display for Alexa for three generations in a row, and the 2023 model remains my preferred option of the Show 8 models, even though there's a newer version. The 8-inch screen is a good size for just about everything, from weather updates to recipes and video chats (thanks to the 13-MP camera), without being overly bulky.

The third-gen model has a smart home hub and spatial audio. I was also happier with the sound quality on this one compared with the newer fourth-gen Echo Show 8 ($200). While the fourth gen comes with Alexa+ right away and has an updated screen experience, the speaker is a little weaker and doesn't have the same bass and depth level to the songs as the third-gen version. The biggest irritation I have with the third-gen version is that Amazon will show lots of ads on it (along with other Echo Show devices), but there are some ways to get around that.

Not only do I love this model, but it hasn't risen in price like the newer Echo Show 8 and other Echo speakers I like, making it a better buy than ever.

While I wouldn't call these smart speakers my absolute favorites from Amazon, they have some excellent qualities that make them stand out among the vast lineup of Echo models.

The Echo Studio (2nd Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for sound quality. This is the second version of the Echo Studio to be our audiophile pick. The current version is a similar size to the old Echo (4th gen), but the musical power on this speaker is almost ridiculous. It filled my entire second floor's long great room with music, and I didn't even need to reach the highest level of volume to pull it off. Honestly, I'm almost afraid to use it at full blast. Not only was it loud, but clear and delivered a nice amount of bass, beautifully playing soft tones of Tracy Chapman's “Fast Car” and the piano riffs of “Dark Blue” by Jack's Mannequin with its three 1.5-inch drivers, plus a 3.75-inch woofer. The harmonizing of “What Is This Feeling?” by Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo sounded beautiful, too. If you're looking for big sound in an Alexa box, this is it. It's a similar size to the Apple HomePod, but I like the sound much better and it's cheaper, too. You'll also get a built-in smart home hub, spatial audio and Dolby Atmos, tap controls like the Echo Dot Max, and early access to Alexa+ right away.

The Echo Spot (2nd Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for bedside tables. The Echo Spot returned in 2024 after a few years of discontinuation, and it's a great little bedside companion thanks to its half-circle screen that displays the time, plus any alarms you have set are also visible under the main time. You can customize the clock with a couple of different color and face options, and the screen dims nicely when the lights are out to a gentle red that's easy to read without lighting up the room. I like asking for alarms set to my latest playlist or some lo-fi jams, and it's easy to set that up with a voice request. Unlike the Echo Shows, it doesn't have a distracting, constantly moving slideshow that would be annoying for the bedroom, nor does it display ads or have a built-in camera. (Nobody wants a rogue camera in their bedroom.) It does not have fantastic sound, but it's plenty loud for an alarm or casual listening while you get dressed in the morning.

The Echo Dot Kids (5th Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for kids. Do your kids really need their own Alexa speaker? That's up to you. This special edition of the Echo Dot is nearly identical to the fifth-gen Dot above, but it has easy-to-use parental controls that allow you to set time limits, filter explicit content, and review activity. The owl- or dragon-themed sphere comes with a year of Amazon Kids+, which includes thousands of Audible books and other special games and features. After that, you'll be charged $3 per month. Alexa can help your kids spell, play their favorite music, or—via another speaker in your house—remind them of dinner time.

There are a lot of Echo devices out there, and some third-party speakers that are Amazon Alexa–compatible. Here are other Alexa smart speakers we've tried and what we thought of them. Some of these speakers haven't increased in price like the models above, which might make them more appealing than before if you're looking to spend less.

Amazon Echo Dot (5th Gen) With Clock for $60: I like this version of the older Echo Dot that adds an LED clock to the front of the speaker, and was thrilled to see it in stock again last year. The LED clock can also display information like the weather when you ask Alexa questions. It's once again temporarily out of stock as of this writing, and has had spotty availability. Still, it's a good find when it's available. There is the new Echo Time ($200) out now too, which will likely eclipse the Dot With Clock in permanent availability.

Amazon Echo Hub for $180: The Amazon Echo Hub is similar to an Echo Show, but prioritizes smart home controls over entertainment. It's a slim device that feels a bit like a tablet, designed to be mounted on the wall (or placed on a separately purchased stand, which is how I used it) and used to control your smart home devices. It's a great choice for anyone who wants something focused on smart home control only. You can still ask Alexa questions and even play music, but the thin speakers aren't worth playing music from. But you can tell your Echo Hub to play music on a different set of speakers, and even set up default speakers to work with it. It's a great companion device if you already have a smart home setup.

Amazon Echo Pop: The Echo Pop is a perfectly fine little speaker, and the cutest one in Amazon's lineup. Does it have great sound? No. It's fine enough for background tunes or if you're limited to a dorm room, but you'll get much better sound for a similar size from the Echo Dot (but you'll pay a little more, and you won't get as cute of colors). It looks like Amazon has it fully out of stock, though, and only Best Buy seems to be carrying it right now, for twice the usual $40 price.

Amazon Echo Show 5 (3rd Gen) for $100: This smart display is another just-fine option, but it's too small to be a great display, and the included camera makes it a no for a bedside table; better to go with the above Echo Spot or an Echo Dot. Amazon did raise the price by $10.

Amazon Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) for $200: I usually love an Echo Show 8, but this model didn't have the same sound quality as the older model. If you're going to get one of Amazon's new displays, you're better off getting the Echo Show 11 ($250) for the same experience with a slightly larger screen (while it's a 3-inch difference, it doesn't feel that big) and better sound. Amazon did raise the price by $20.

Amazon Echo Show 15 (2nd Gen) for $350: This smart display is good, but it clearly wants to double as a TV and isn't very good at it yet. I'm hoping we see better TV-related performance in the future to make it worth adding to a kitchen or office. It does a great job with widgets, though, thanks to the massive 15.6-inch screen. There's also the larger Echo Show 21 ($500), which is essentially the same thing but larger. Both of these large displays rose in price—the Show 15 went up $50, while the Show 21 went up $100.

JBL Authentics 200 for $200: This JBL smart speaker supports both Google Assistant and Amazon Alexa, letting you switch between them for different tasks without changing your preference in the app. That makes this speaker particularly appealing for folks with a sprawling collection of smart products from both.

Sonos Era 100 for $219: If you're looking for a speaker that can talk to Alexa but isn't necessarily made by Amazon, the Sonos Era 100 is a great option. We just wish we liked the Sonos app better. You can catch our entire guide to the Sonos ecosystem here.

Amazon announced several new Echo models at the end of October that promise a richer Alexa+ experience. Some of these are new models of Echo speakers we've seen before, and some are entirely new. Here are all the new models, prices, and their standout features I'll be testing:

There's also the Alexa Photo Frame ($230), which will be a digital photo frame with Alexa+ built in. I haven't loved Amazon's past photo uploading experience for making its smart displays into photo frames, but I'll be testing it soon to see what the experience is like for a dedicated photo device. You'll be able to command Alexa+ on this device, but I hesitate to call it a speaker, since it doesn't sound designed for listening to music. Still, it's one of the new Alexa devices I'm most intrigued by, and it's available now.

Amazon raised many of its prices in August on its products, affecting the Amazon Echo line as well as Kindles, Fire TV streaming sticks, and Eero routers. It wasn't a huge surprise, as many companies have done this recently, citing rising costs and chip shortages, but this price hike happened ahead of Amazon launching new lines for most of these products, so it was likely to establish higher prices for the new lineup. Still, it's disappointing to see and will lead to a fall sale season with prices that won't be as impressive as earlier this summer.

Amazon's Echo devices saw increases from anywhere between $20 and $100, with the larger price increases being for the Echo Shows. The following Echo speakers all faced a price increase:

Amazon has rolled out the new-and-improved Amazon Alexa, named Alexa+, which is built on generative AI and promises a more powerful assistant that can handle more conversational topics and requests. It's available for a free 30-day trial; after that, you either pay a $20 monthly fee or become a Prime member. Being a Prime member is the better deal, likely by design. Neither my colleagues nor I have been impressed enough by Alexa+ to say it's worth paying for on its own. I do like the updated, more conversational voice, and Alexa+ did a good job answering all kinds of questions quickly and thoughtfully. Check out our early access hands-on for everything I thought while testing.

What’s the Difference Between an Echo and an Echo Show?

The best time to buy any Amazon speaker is during a major sale event like Black Friday or Amazon Prime Day, when there are often steep discounts. You'll often see the cheaper speakers for around 50 percent off, and the larger speakers see some nice sale prices, too.

How and Where Should You Set Up Your Alexa?

Ultimately, what's most important is that the speaker is somewhere it can hear your commands. Where that will be will vary based on your home, but think about where you'll be when you ask for the weather or to dim the lights, and place your speaker accordingly.

You'll set up Alexa speakers using the Alexa app, which allows you to manage multiple Alexa speakers linked to your Amazon account. Third-party speaker setup methods may vary.

Alexa is always listening, to a certain extent. It's designed to only listen for its wake word and shouldn't be recording or processing any audio unless it hears that word. But Alexa can sometimes mishear a word and think it's the wake word, or it might hear a word similar enough to activate the speaker. If you've owned an Alexa, there have likely been times when the assistant suddenly responds when you weren't speaking to it. Once it hears the wake word (or what it believes to be the wake word), it will start listening to everything in an attempt to hear what you need and respond.

Alexa+, the latest version of Alexa, will also remain on for a little bit after you ask a question to listen for follow-up questions, no wake word required. Both Alexa and Alexa+ light up in some fashion (regular speakers will turn the light ring blue, while the displays will have a blue bar appear on the screen) to let you know the assistant is listening. Most Echo devices also have a physical mute button and will display a red light or red bar to let you know when the mute is activated.

How Do You Remove Unwanted Content From an Echo Show?

If you're using an Echo Show device, you've likely noticed there is a ton of default content the device will show you. Sports scores! Local news! A recipe you might be interested in! It makes the device exhausting and annoying to be near.

Can I Have My Alexa Requests Locally Processed, or Do They Have to Go to the Cloud?

How Does WIRED Select Smart Speakers to Test? How Are These Speakers Tested?

For this guide, we specifically test speakers that are compatible with Amazon Alexa. It's a big limitation and narrows down the options significantly, especially compared to speaker options you'll see in our other guides like the Best Bluetooth Speakers. That's mainly Amazon's own ecosystem of speakers, and while there are third-party options, the best options tend to be of Amazon's own design to work with its own voice assistant.

Each speaker gets installed in a tester's home for day-to-day use, to see how the microphone performs, how the speaker sounds with different types of music, how well the smart home control features work with compatible devices such as smart lights and video doorbells, and to test other features as necessary (e.g., streaming features on smart displays).

How Does WIRED Get Models? What Does WIRED Do After Testing Them?

We usually obtain review units as press samples, though we will also independently purchase samples if need be. Any units were provided with no obligation to cover or promises for what that coverage would be.

After testing, we keep most of our picks either installed for long-term testing in our homes or in storage to compare against updated models and new speakers that come out. If the sample becomes irrelevant or unnecessary to keep, we donate it locally.

#482. Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on November 2, 2026

The Moon has now reached its Waning Crescent phase, which means less than half of its surface illuminated. It will continue to decrease now until we reach the New Moon.

As of Monday, Nov. 2, NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waning Crescent phase, with 45% of its surface visible.

Tonight, without the use of visual aids you should be able to spot the Tycho Crater, Kepler Crater, and the Mare Imbrium. Binoculars will also help you see the Alphonsus Crater, the Clavius Crater, and the Grimaldi Basin. And, if you have access to a telescope, you'll also see the Apollo 12 landing spot, the Reiner Gamma, and the Schiller Crater.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

The Moon takes approximately 29.5 days to complete an orbit around Earth, going through a series of phases along the way. Depending on its position relative to Earth and the Sun, the amount of its illuminated surface we can see changes, creating the familiar sequence of crescents, quarter moons and the Full Moon. Once the cycle is complete, the pattern repeats, as explained by NASA.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere)

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

#481. Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany's health scare highlights the need for better support for elite coaches

Vincent Kompany’s health concern is a reminder that elite football's pressures affect coaches too. Better support, clearer structures and mental health safeguards are increasingly vital.

Vincent Kompany has just returned home from hospital. The Bayern Munich head coach admitted that he hadn't listened to his body, "and then at some point, my body just said, 'Enough is enough!'"

Bayern Munich's sporting director Max Eberl, who left Gladbach in 2022 due to his own health concerns, told German public broadcaster ARD that the 40-year-old Belgian had been suffering from meningeal irritation, which if untreated can become meningitis.

"They found out what it is. It is a meningeal irritation that brought on the incident last Friday," said Eberl, referring to when Kompany collapsed during training and required an emergency doctor.

"Honestly, he is doing as well as can be expected. He has been discharged from hospital today, which is the biggest and best news for all of us."

The news has been met by great concern from the German football community. Bayern fans held a banner showing their support, many German media outlets wrote opinion articles softly reminding that coaches are humans too and they too need support. Even the wider coaching community has started to ask questions.

"It’s something you take to heart and think about," Freiburg head coach Julian Schuster said after his team lost to Bayern recently.

"We coaches aren’t always very good at taking care of ourselves in those situations."

Eberl, though, shut down the suggestion that this was related to pressure or stress.

"It's an illness. Any one of us can get it. It has nothing to do with the pressure we face in the Bundesliga," Eberl said.

Nevertheless, with Kompany admitting he hadn't listened to his body and his assistant coach Aaron Danks saying that "getting Vince to rest is a challenge", it is clear that the Belgian had been working very hard of late.

Kompany, whose father became the first Black mayor in Belgium after moving there from the DR Congo, has faced an enormous amount of adversity in his life. At just 14, his parents divorced and he told The Guardian in a 2019 interview: "I need to be fed stuff constantly, otherwise I don’t know how to function. I can't remember a lazy Sunday."

The Belgian's own history, both in his childhood and as former professional player, also plays a role in understanding the challenges coaches face in elite sport.

"I think we (coaches) have a really poor measure of ourselves within this example of like, wasn't listening to my body. I think a lot of coaches are really poor at that,"  coaching mentor Cody Royle, who has worked with teams in the NBA and the Premier League, told DW.

"And so part of my role is to enhance their attunement to that, to ask questions to that effect, to try to perhaps even impart some things that I've learned along the way or heard from others or other coaches that are going through similar things so that you can actually start to put words to what that feeling might have been or where you maybe touched burnout but it didn't quite get there and you're able to rescue something and start to really develop skill within it," he said.

"I think with Vincent's example we also need to account for the fact that this is a young man still finding his way in coaching and so he's still understanding what those triggers are within his body and what they're really telling him Maybe he had physical things that he could read when he was playing. These are more mental triggers, and he's still learning that and that's part of what he needs to do. But there should be people around that help."

It begs the question, in 2026, at a time when awareness around mental and physical health is greater than ever, particularly in elite sport, how is this still possible?

"I suspect that many head coaches aren't able to let go or delegate," Frank Wormuth, an educator for the German Football Association (DFB), told DW.

"They want to control everything because they don't feel secure when the team loses," continued Wormuth, adding that that's why coaches often bring close friends into their staff.

"You'd think professional coaches wouldn't have to worry, since they've earned enough money, but that’s not a good coach's priority—success is far more important."

A former coach, Wormuth admits that he had moments in his career when he had lost sight of how much of a role football was playing in his life.

"I never felt like I was doing too much until my kids pointed out to me—when I was at home—that I wasn't the coach anymore, but should be fulfilling the role of a father," Wormuth said.

"That's when I realized that I was truly operating 24/7 as a coach in my head, even when I was at home."

To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio

Royle believes coaches need to learn more about how to manage themselves.

"I kind of throw my hands up a little bit at the fact that we aren't further along," Royle said.

"We're not even trying to educate this in to our young coaches as they come through. The education system probably facilitates this as much as the organizations that are individually responsible."

Clearly, if not well managed, extremely demanding elite-sports environments with high expectations on individuals makes for a dangerous combination. Both Wormuth and Royle advocate for the concept of a second set of eyes.

"Maybe it is that there's a mechanism now for coaches to really investigate," Royle said.

Having someone who sits outside the organization and doesn't belong to the politics to be able to —whether it's on the phone or come in for a visit — just say, 'You need to go home because this isn't going well.'"

"This is a game where Jock Stein literally dropped dead on the sideline, right? There shouldn't need to be any more conversation beyond that... and it was workaholism and stress that caused it," added Royle.

"So I don't know what else it's going to take, but I just don't think the game really cares enough to change anything about it. The show must go on, right?"

Even as it does when Bayern Munich play Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga's most marketed game this weekend, Kompany's absence will serve as a reminder that while much of the focus of modern sport is on the players, there is an equal level of support required for those on the sidelines.
